title: The microbes who live on you and in you: many lands on one body

summary.text: The bacteria between your toes are different from the bacteria on your forearm, though both places are your own skin. Why? In this lesson you swab three places on your skin and grow what you find on potato slices. You play a dice game that shows how the microbes who live in you keep harmful newcomers out. You also find out why the same microbe can help in one place and harm in another.
summary.art: A child sitting on the floor looking at her own forearm through a magnifying glass, with four sealed bags holding potato slices beside her.

intro.hook: Your forearm and the gap between your toes are less than a metre apart, and both are covered by your own skin. Yet different microbes live in each. How can one body be so many different homes?
intro.text: A microbe is a living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are the commonest microbes on you. About 38 trillion bacteria live on and in a grown-up, and nearly all of them are harmless or helpful. They do not live evenly spread. A dry forearm, an oily forehead, a damp toe gap, a mouth and a large intestine each give different food, water and air. So each holds a different community. In this lesson you test that yourself. You rub clean cotton buds on three places on your skin and grow what they pick up. You play Hold the Space, a dice game about how the microbes who already live in a gut keep a harmful newcomer out. By the end you can explain why most microbes do you no harm. You can also explain when a harmless microbe becomes a harmful one.
intro.art: A child's body drawn as a simple map, with the forearm coloured like dry sand, the forehead shiny yellow and the toe gaps deep green.

outcomes: By the end I can say what residents and visitors are, and name the main places on and in a body where microbes live.
By the end I can explain why different parts of one body hold different microbes, using water, oil, acid and oxygen.
By the end I can run a fair swab test on potato slices, and say what the test can and cannot show.
By the end I can use a dice model to explain how residents keep a harmful newcomer out.
By the end I can explain why most microbes are harmless or helpful, and why the same microbe can help in one place and harm in another.
By the end I can say where a baby's microbes come from, and how food, people, pets and medicines change the community.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about or do not know about the microbes who live with us.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, yeasts and many other tiny beings are microbes.
terms.example: One full stop on this page could hold thousands of bacteria side by side.
terms.art: A full stop on a printed page with a circle zooming in to show many tiny rod and ball shapes.

terms.meaning: Microbes made of one small cell each. One of them is called a bacterium. They are the commonest living beings on and in your body.
terms.example: The bacteria in your large intestine break down plant fibre that your own cells leave whole.
terms.art: A few rod-shaped and round bacteria drawn large, each with a thin outer wall.

terms.meaning: A microbe who lives and multiplies on a body for a long time. Residents live in the pores of the skin, in the mouth and in the gut.
terms.example: Soap and water lift off dirt, but the residents deep in your skin pores stay and grow back within hours.
terms.art: A cross-section of skin with a hair pore, and small dots living deep inside the pore.

terms.meaning: A microbe who lands on a body from soil, food, a door handle or another person, and stays only a short time.
terms.example: Soil bacteria picked up on your fingers in a flower pot wash off with soap.
terms.art: A child's hand with a few dots sitting loosely on the surface of the fingertips after touching a flower pot.

terms.meaning: All the different living beings who share one place and affect each other.
terms.example: The bacteria, yeasts and tiny mites on a grown-up's forehead make up one community.
terms.art: A circle showing several different shapes of microbes living side by side on a patch of skin.

terms.meaning: The whole community of microbes who live on and in one body, or in one part of a body.
terms.example: Your gut microbiome is the community of microbes in your stomach and intestines.
terms.art: An outline of a child with clouds of small coloured dots over the mouth, the skin and the belly.

terms.meaning: The place where a living being lives, with the food, water, air and warmth found there.
terms.example: The gap between two toes is a warm, damp habitat. The forearm is a dry one.
terms.art: A forearm drawn beside a dry sandy landscape, and a toe gap drawn beside a wet green forest.

terms.meaning: The oil that skin makes in tiny glands beside each hair. It keeps skin soft and is food for some bacteria and yeasts.
terms.example: A grown-up's forehead and nose feel slightly oily by evening because of sebum.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a hair in the skin with a small gland beside the hair making drops of oil.

terms.meaning: A clean cotton bud rubbed on a surface to pick up the microbes there. To swab is to rub with one.
terms.example: In the Three Lands Test you swab your forearm, your forehead and a toe gap.
terms.art: A hand rubbing a cotton bud between two toes.

terms.meaning: A spot you can see, made of millions of microbes who all grew from one or a few cells that landed there.
terms.example: One cream-coloured dot on a potato slice is a colony.
terms.art: A potato slice with several round dots in cream, yellow and white, and one dot zoomed in to show packed tiny cells.

terms.meaning: A microbe who lives without oxygen. For many anaerobes, oxygen is a poison.
terms.example: Most bacteria in the large intestine are anaerobes, so they cannot be grown on a slice left in the air.
terms.art: A cut-away of a large intestine with many bacteria inside and a sign showing oxygen crossed out.

terms.meaning: A slippery layer that the body makes to cover its wet inner surfaces, such as the nose and the gut wall.
terms.example: Gut bacteria live in and on the mucus that lines the large intestine, and some eat it.
terms.art: A gut wall drawn with a thick jelly-like layer on top, and bacteria sitting on the outer part of the layer.

terms.meaning: The way residents keep newcomers out by already using the room and the food, and by making substances that newcomers dislike. Scientists call it colonisation resistance.
terms.example: In the Hold the Space game, a newcomer who lands on a square with a resident finds no room.
terms.art: A grid full of small grains with one larger bean hovering above and finding no empty square.

terms.meaning: An everyday word for a microbe who makes someone ill. The science word is pathogen.
terms.example: The bacterium who causes cholera is a germ. The bacteria who set curd are not.
terms.art: A glass of unclean water with one comma-shaped bacterium circled in red.

terms.meaning: A microbe who lives harmlessly in one part of a body but causes illness when she reaches another part, or when the body's defences are low.
terms.example: A gut bacterium who gets into the bladder can cause a painful infection there.
terms.art: An outline of a belly with an arrow showing a bacterium moving from the intestine to the bladder, where she is marked in red.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them multiplying. An antibiotic does not work on viruses.
terms.example: An antibiotic for an ear infection also kills many harmless bacteria in the gut.
terms.art: A strip of tablets beside an outline of a gut in which some of the dots have faded.

terms.meaning: The way a community in a new place changes in steps, as the first settlers are joined and replaced by others.
terms.example: A baby's gut is settled first by a few kinds of bacteria, and by many more kinds after the first solid food.
terms.art: Three small panels showing a bare rock, then moss, then bushes, beside three panels of a baby's gut with a few, then more, then many kinds of dots.

terms.meaning: Single-celled microbes who look like bacteria but belong to a separate great branch of life.
terms.example: An archaeon in the human gut uses up hydrogen gas and makes methane.
terms.art: Two similar-looking tiny cells side by side, labelled as a bacterium and an archaeon, on two separate branches of a tree.

terms.meaning: The way bacteria sense how many of their own kind are near. Each one gives out a signal substance, and all of them change what they do when the signal is strong.
terms.example: Light-making bacteria in a squid start to glow only when enough of them are crowded together.
terms.art: A small squid with a glowing patch on the underside, and a zoom-in of many bacteria passing small dots to each other.

terms.meaning: Finding out who lives in a sample by reading the DNA in the sample, without growing anything.
terms.example: Reading genes found many kinds of gut bacteria that nobody had ever grown on a dish.
terms.art: A swab beside a machine printing a long strip of the letters A, T, G and C.

explanations.concept: Residents and visitors: who lives on a body
explanations.definition: A resident is a microbe who lives and multiplies on or in a body for months or years. A visitor is a microbe who lands there and is gone within hours or days. All of a body's microbes together are called the microbiome.
explanations.description: Every healthy person, dog, crow and earthworm carries microbes. A grown-up human carries about 38 trillion bacteria, which is about as many as the body's own cells. All of them together weigh about 200 grams, the weight of a small mango. They are light because a bacterium is far smaller than a human cell. Besides bacteria there are yeasts, archaea and viruses, and on most grown-ups some tiny mites as well. Residents hold on. Skin residents live deep in the pores, where a wash does not reach, and they spread back over the skin within hours. Visitors come from soil, food, door handles and other people. Most visitors find the place too dry, too acid or too crowded, and they die or are washed off. Why does this matter? Because hand washing is aimed at visitors. Soap lifts off the visitors, among whom the germs are found, and the residents remain.
examples: After you repot a plant, soil bacteria are visitors on your fingers. Soap and water remove most of them.
The bacteria in the pores of your forearm are residents. They were there last month and will be there next month.
A dog who lives in your home leaves visitors on your skin every day. Some of them may settle.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in patch of skin with dots living deep in a pore, labelled residents, and loose dots on the surface, labelled visitors.

explanations.concept: Your skin is three kinds of land: dry, damp and oily
explanations.definition: Skin is not the same everywhere. Some parts are dry, some are damp, and some are oily. Each kind of skin holds a different community of microbes.
explanations.description: In 2009 Elizabeth Grice, Julia Segre and their team in the United States swabbed 20 places on the skin of 10 healthy people. They read the genes of the bacteria in each swab. They found that the places fell into three groups. Oily places, such as the forehead and the sides of the nose, were home mostly to bacteria who eat skin oil. Damp places, such as the armpit, the elbow crease and the toe gaps, held bacteria who need water. Dry places, such as the forearm and the palm, held a mixed crowd, with many kinds but few of each. Why would this be so? A microbe needs water and food. Sweat gives water and salts. Oil glands give sebum. A dry forearm gives little of either, and flakes of dead skin fall off all day and carry bacteria away with them. The team wrote that a hairy, damp underarm and a smooth, dry forearm are as different for microbes as a rainforest and a desert. The same year, Elizabeth Costello and her team compared up to 27 places on several people. The place on the body told them more about the community than the person did.
examples: A grown-up's forehead is oily, and the commonest bacteria there live deep in the oil pores.
The gaps between your toes are warm and damp inside socks and shoes, and they hold many bacteria and many kinds of fungi.
Your forearm is dry. Fewer bacteria live there, but they are of many different kinds.
explanations.art: A body outline coloured in three colours: yellow for oily places, blue for damp places and brown for dry places.

explanations.concept: Children's skin and grown-ups' skin hold different residents
explanations.definition: The skin community changes as a person grows. Skin makes much more oil from about the age of 10 to 13, and the oil-eating bacteria become common only then.
explanations.description: The bacterium who is commonest on a grown-up's forehead is called Cutibacterium acnes. They live deep in the hair pores, where there is little oxygen, and they eat sebum. On the skin of healthy children who have not yet reached their teens, they are hard to find at all. The reason is food. A child's oil glands make little sebum. In the early teens the glands begin to make much more, and the oil-eaters multiply. In 2012 Julia Oh and her team compared children and grown-ups aged 2 to 40. The children carried different bacteria from the grown-ups, most clearly inside the nose. Sweat changes too. Sweat on a child's forehead is mostly water and salt. From the teens, glands in the armpit add other substances, which armpit bacteria turn into smelly ones. So a body is a different habitat at different ages. That is one reason why your forehead swab may grow less than a grown-up's would.
examples: Sweat has no smell when it is fresh. Bacteria in a grown-up's armpit change substances in the sweat into smelly ones.
Foot bacteria make the cheesy smell of shoes worn all day. Relatives of the same bacteria give some strong cheeses their smell.
A baby, a ten-year-old and a grandmother in one home each carry a different skin community.
explanations.art: Three faces side by side, a small child, a teenager and a grown-up, with more and more shine drawn on the forehead.

explanations.concept: Why the potato slice shows only some of them
explanations.definition: A potato slice in the air grows only the microbes who can eat potato, live in oxygen and multiply quickly. Many residents of the body need something else, so they never show up as spots.
explanations.description: Each spot on your slice is a colony. It began as one cell, or a few, who landed there and multiplied until millions made a dot you can see. A cell who cannot use potato or who needs a place without oxygen never makes a dot. The oil-eating bacteria of the forehead are like that. So are most bacteria of the large intestine, for whom oxygen is a poison. This means a slice with few spots does not prove that few microbes lived on that skin. It shows how many of the kind who like potato and air were there. Scientists met the same problem. For about a hundred years they knew only the microbes who grew on their dishes. Today they read the genes in a swab instead, which finds the ones who will not grow. The newer method has limits too. Genes show who is there, but not always who is alive or what they are doing.
examples: A swab from an oily forehead may grow few spots on potato, although millions of oil-eaters live in the pores there.
In 1999 scientists compared the two methods on plaque from below one man's gums. Growing found 28 kinds. Reading genes found 59.
About three in ten of the kinds of microbes known from the human mouth have never been grown in a laboratory.
explanations.art: A potato slice with a few spots beside a strip of DNA letters listing many more names, with a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: The mouth: several habitats within one hand's width
explanations.definition: The mouth has hard teeth, a rough tongue, smooth cheeks and narrow gaps under the gums. Each surface holds a different community.
explanations.description: More than 500 kinds of microbes are known from the human mouth. They do not mix evenly. The top of the tongue is a rough carpet with deep folds. Bacteria who need little oxygen live at the bottom of the folds. A tooth is the only hard surface in the body that is never shed, so a film can build up on a tooth for days. The cheeks shed their top cells all the time, and each cell carries bacteria away as you swallow. Saliva washes through all the time. A microbe who cannot hold on is swallowed and meets the acid of the stomach. In 2016 Jessica Mark Welch and her team coloured each kind of bacterium in tooth film with a different glowing dye. Under the microscope they saw order. Long thread-shaped bacteria stood up from the tooth like the spines of a hedgehog. Other kinds sat at the tips, in the open, and kinds who avoid oxygen sat deep inside. Those who make a waste substance sat beside those who eat that substance. Even a film too thin to see clearly has its own neighbourhoods.
examples: Your tongue feels rough because of many tiny bumps. The folds between them shelter bacteria.
The film on a tooth is thickest along the gum, where the tongue and the brush reach least.
Bacteria on the cheek are swallowed as the cheek cells they sit on come loose.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a mouth with the tongue, a tooth, the cheek and the gum edge each labelled, and a different pattern of dots on each.

explanations.concept: From the stomach to the large intestine: acid, speed and no oxygen
explanations.definition: The food tube changes along its length. The stomach is very acid. The small intestine moves fast. The large intestine is slow and has no oxygen. So the number of microbes rises from a few thousand in a millilitre in the stomach to about a hundred billion in the large intestine.
explanations.description: Follow a mouthful down. Saliva holds about a billion bacteria in each millilitre, and you swallow them all day. Stomach acid kills most of them. A millilitre of stomach contents holds only a few thousand bacteria. The upper small intestine is also thinly settled, because food rushes through, and bile, a digestive juice from the liver, harms many bacteria. Lower down the flow slows and the numbers climb. In the large intestine, the leftovers stay for a day or more. It is warm, wet, full of plant fibre and has no oxygen. About a hundred billion bacteria live in each millilitre there. So nearly all of your 38 trillion bacteria are in the large intestine. The whole of your skin holds perhaps a hundred billion, which is less than one part in three hundred. Most of the gut residents are anaerobes. They break down fibre that your own body leaves whole, and the cells of the gut wall use what the bacteria leave over. Archaea live there too. One kind uses up the hydrogen gas that the fibre-eaters give off, and makes methane.
examples: One bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, lives in the stomach. She burrows into the mucus on the stomach wall and makes a substance that weakens the acid around her.
Nearly all of the 38 trillion bacteria in a grown-up are in the large intestine.
Much of the gas a person passes is made by gut microbes as they break down fibre.
explanations.art: A food tube drawn from mouth to large intestine, with very few dots in the stomach, more in the small intestine and a dense crowd in the large intestine.

explanations.concept: Places with few microbes, or none
explanations.definition: Healthy blood, muscle and brain have no microbes living in them. Some places once thought to be free of microbes, such as the lungs, hold small numbers.
explanations.description: Your skin and the lining of your gut are walls. Microbes live on the outer side of the walls. On the inner side, in the blood and the organs, defence cells remove any microbe who gets through. That is why a bacterium who is harmless on the skin can be dangerous in a deep cut. Some places are not as simple as the old books said. Textbooks used to say that healthy lungs have no bacteria. Reading genes showed that healthy lungs hold small, changing numbers, breathed in from the mouth and cleared again. Urine in the bladder was also called free of microbes. In 2014 a team in the United States used better ways of growing. They found living bacteria in most of the urine samples they tested, from women with and without bladder trouble. Whether an unborn baby meets any microbes in the womb is still argued about. Most scientists now think that a healthy womb has none, and that earlier findings were probably traces picked up during the testing.
examples: A splinter pushes skin bacteria through the wall, so the place may turn red and sore.
Doctors clean the skin before an injection, so that the needle does not carry skin residents into the body.
The inside of a healthy muscle has no microbes at all.
explanations.art: An outline of a body with the skin and food tube marked with dots, and the heart, muscles and brain left clear.

explanations.concept: A newborn is new land: where your microbes came from
explanations.definition: A baby meets her first microbes at birth. Over about three years the gut community changes in steps, from a few kinds to many. This step-by-step change is called succession.
explanations.description: In 2010 Maria Gloria Dominguez-Bello and her team swabbed mothers and their babies within minutes of birth. They found something striking. The mothers had different communities on the skin, in the mouth and in the birth passage. Each newborn carried nearly the same community all over the body. So the lands of the body sort the microbes afterwards. Babies born through the birth passage first carried bacteria from there. Babies born by an operation first carried bacteria like those of skin. Later studies found that these differences become smaller as the child grows, and babies born either way grow up healthy. Then comes milk. Mother's milk holds special sugars that a baby cannot digest at all. They are the third largest solid part of the milk, after milk sugar and fat. Why would a mother make food her baby cannot use? Because the sugars are food for certain bacteria, called Bifidobacterium, in the baby's gut. The first solid food brings fibre, and fibre-eating bacteria move in. A study of 903 children found three steps. The community changes fast until about 14 months. It settles slowly until about 30 months. After that it stays steady.
examples: In many Indian families a baby's first rice is a ceremony: choroonu in Kerala, annaprashan in Bengal. That spoonful is also the first rice for the baby's gut bacteria.
A baby who puts a toy, a toe and the floor into her mouth is meeting visitors from the home.
By about three years old, a child's gut community looks much like a grown-up's.
explanations.art: A strip of four panels: a newborn with one kind of dot all over, a baby drinking milk, a baby eating rice, and a three-year-old with many kinds of dots in the belly.

explanations.concept: Holding the space: how residents keep newcomers out
explanations.definition: A harmful microbe who arrives on a body must find room and food. Residents already use both, and some make substances that stop newcomers. This is called colonisation resistance, or holding the space.
explanations.description: Think of a full bus. A new passenger finds no seat. Residents hold the space in three ways. First, they cover the surface, so a newcomer finds nowhere to hold on. Second, they eat the food, so little is left. Third, many of them make substances that harm other microbes. In 2016 a team in Germany studied a bacterium who lives in some people's noses, called Staphylococcus lugdunensis. She makes a substance that kills Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium who can cause serious wound infections. In the team's hospital samples, people who carried the first bacterium rarely carried the second. In 2017 Teruaki Nakatsuji and his team found skin residents who make substances that kill the same harmful bacterium. People with the skin illness eczema had few of these residents. The gut shows the idea most clearly. A long course of antibiotics can kill so many gut residents that one tough bacterium, called Clostridioides difficile, multiplies and causes severe diarrhoea. In 2013 doctors in the Netherlands treated such patients by putting gut bacteria from a healthy person into their intestine. It cured 13 of 16 patients at the first try. An antibiotic alone cured 4 of 13.
examples: In the Hold the Space game, the same dice rolls give a newcomer almost no squares on a full board and many squares on a nearly empty one.
Bacteria in the birth passage make acid, and the acid keeps most other microbes from settling.
After a course of antibiotics some people get a sore white coating in the mouth. A yeast who was already there has multiplied, because the bacteria around the yeast were killed.
explanations.art: Two grids side by side: one full of small grains with a bean bouncing off, and one nearly empty with beans spreading across.

explanations.concept: Most microbes are harmless: counting the kinds
explanations.definition: Of all the kinds of microbes on Earth, only a small number can make a human ill. Most kinds never live on us at all, and most of those who do cause no harm.
explanations.description: In 2001 three scientists went through the medical books and listed every kind of living being and virus known to make humans ill. They counted 1,415 kinds. Of these, 538 were bacteria, 307 were fungi, 217 were viruses and prions, 66 were single-celled beings called protozoa, and 287 were worms. Now compare. More than 500 kinds of microbes live in human mouths alone. About a thousand kinds of bacteria have been found on healthy human skin. Soil and sea hold far more kinds, and most have no name yet. So the germs are a short list beside a very long one. Why are so few harmful? To make someone ill, a microbe must get past the skin or gut wall, find food there, and survive the body's defences. Most microbes are built for soil, water or a leaf, and a warm human body is the wrong place for them. But harmless does not mean helpful. Many microbes on us seem to do nothing for us. They simply live there.
examples: The bacteria who set curd, raise idli batter and rot a fallen leaf never make a healthy person ill.
A spoon of garden soil holds billions of bacteria, and almost none of them can live in a human.
Of the microbes who do live on us, a few are helpers, a few are sometimes harmful, and many are passengers who neither help nor harm.
explanations.art: A long row of small squares coloured green with a short row of red squares beside it, to compare harmless kinds with harmful kinds.

explanations.concept: Helper, passenger or trouble: the same microbe in a different place
explanations.definition: Many microbes are not simply good or bad. The same bacterium can be harmless in one part of the body and cause illness in another part. Such a microbe is called an opportunist.
explanations.description: Take the gut bacterium Escherichia coli. In the large intestine most kinds of this bacterium live quietly. If the same bacterium reaches the bladder, she can multiply there and cause a painful infection. She is the commonest cause of bladder infections. Or take Staphylococcus aureus. About one person in four carries this bacterium in the nose and never knows. In a deep wound or in the blood, the same bacterium is dangerous. Three things decide what happens. The first is the place. The second is the number, as when a film on a tooth grows thick. The third is the state of the body, as when someone is very ill or very old. This changes how we should think about germs. A few microbes, such as the cholera bacterium, harm us wherever they grow in us. For many others, 'germ' describes a microbe in the wrong place or at the wrong time. This is also why the walls of the body matter so much. Clean hands before eating, and a washed and covered cut, keep microbes in the places where they do no harm.
examples: Gut bacteria that leak into the belly through a burst appendix cause a dangerous infection, so doctors operate quickly.
A skin bacterium who is harmless on the arm can cause illness when she grows on a plastic tube put into a hospital patient's vein.
The bacteria who make acid on teeth do little harm in a thin film. In a thick film fed with sweets all day, they cause holes.
explanations.art: The same rod-shaped bacterium drawn twice, once in a gut marked with a green tick and once in a bladder marked with a red cross.

explanations.concept: What an antibiotic does to the residents
explanations.definition: An antibiotic kills bacteria. A medicine swallowed for an infection in the ear or chest also reaches the gut, and kills many residents there. Most of them grow back within weeks, and a few may not.
explanations.description: In 2008 Les Dethlefsen and his team studied three healthy grown-ups who took an antibiotic for five days. They read the genes of the gut bacteria before, during and after. About a third of the kinds of bacteria became rarer or disappeared from the samples. Four weeks after the medicine ended, each person's community looked close to how it had started. But a few kinds had still not come back after six months. Does this mean antibiotics are bad? No. Antibiotics have saved many millions of lives, and an infection that needs one must be treated. It means an antibiotic is a strong tool with a cost, to be used when a doctor says it is needed. It does nothing against colds and flu, which are caused by viruses. Taking one for a cold harms the residents and does not touch the virus. How best to help the residents grow back is not settled. In one study in 2018, people who took a probiotic after antibiotics got their own community back more slowly than people who took nothing.
examples: Loose stools during a course of antibiotics are common, because many gut residents have been killed.
A doctor who says a cold needs no antibiotic is protecting the child's residents as well as the medicine's power.
An antibiotic cream on a small skin infection reaches far fewer residents than a tablet that travels through the whole gut.
explanations.art: Three drawings of the same gut: crowded with many kinds of dots, thinned out during the medicine, and nearly full again four weeks later with a few kinds missing.

explanations.concept: People who live together share microbes, and so do their dogs
explanations.definition: Microbes pass between bodies all day by touch, by shared things and through the air. People in one home carry more of the same skin microbes than strangers do.
explanations.description: In 2013 Se Jin Song and her team sampled the skin, mouths and guts of 60 families, some with children and some with dogs. People in one home shared more microbes with each other than with people from other homes. The sharing was strongest on the skin. Grown-ups who had a dog shared more skin microbes with each other. They also shared more with their own dog than with other dogs. In 2014 a team in the Netherlands found that partners have more similar tongue communities than strangers do. They also measured that one ten-second kiss passes about 80 million bacteria. In 2015 James Meadow and his team sat people one at a time in a cleaned chamber and sampled the air. A person gives off more than a million tiny particles every hour, many of them carrying bacteria. The team could tell an occupied chamber from an empty one within four hours. They could even tell some people apart by the cloud alone. Do the shared microbes settle, or are they only passing? The scientists said plainly that they do not know yet.
examples: Your skin community is more like your sister's than like that of a child in another city.
A family dog who sleeps on the sofa carries skin microbes from one family member to the next.
When you leave a room, some of your bacteria stay behind on the chair and in the dust.
explanations.art: A family of four and a dog on a sofa, with thin dotted lines linking their hands, the dog's fur and the cushions.

explanations.definition: Every animal who has been studied carries microbes, and many animals depend on particular ones. Some young animals take their microbes from their elders on purpose.
explanations.description: No animal makes the tools to break down the tough walls of plant cells. Plant-eaters depend on gut microbes who do. A cow keeps hers in a large first stomach chamber, the rumen. A termite keeps hers in the hind gut, and they digest the wood she eats. An elephant calf is born without the microbes who break down plants. Elephant calves eat the fresh dung of their mothers and other elders. People who raise orphan calves say this helps a healthy community settle in the gut. They give the calves dung from healthy grown-up elephants. One of the best-studied partnerships is in the sea off Hawaii. The bobtail squid is about 3 centimetres long. She has a pouch on her underside filled with bacteria who make light. At night the glow from below hides her shadow from fish hunting beneath her. Margaret McFall-Ngai and Edward Ruby have studied her for more than thirty years. A newly hatched squid has no bacteria. Within about half a day she has gathered the right kind from seawater, where that kind is rare among millions of others. Every dawn she pushes most of them out, and the rest multiply through the day.
examples: A cow chewing cud is breaking grass into small pieces for the microbes in her rumen.
A termite can live on wood only because of the microbes in her gut.
A bobtail squid without her light-making bacteria casts a shadow on a moonlit night.
explanations.art: An elephant calf reaching with her trunk towards fresh dung beside her mother, and a small glowing squid in a corner of the picture.

explanations.concept: Bacteria sense their neighbours and act together
explanations.definition: Bacteria sense what is around them and change what they do. Many kinds also sense how many of their own kind are near, and act as a group once there are enough. This is called quorum sensing.
explanations.description: Bacteria sense and decide. A bacterium has sensors in her outer skin for sugar, acid, oxygen and many other things, and she swims towards what she needs. Bacteria also keep track of each other. In 1970 Kenneth Nealson, Terry Platt and Woodland Hastings were studying light-making sea bacteria. A few bacteria in a flask stayed dark. Once the flask was crowded, all of them lit up together. Each bacterium gives out a little of a signal substance. When many are near, the signal is strong, and each one switches on the genes for making light. One bacterium alone would waste her food by glowing. A crowd in a squid's pouch makes a useful lamp. Bonnie Bassler later showed that many kinds of bacteria talk this way. Some use one signal for their own kind and another that is shared between kinds. The bacteria on your teeth and in your gut use such signals too. Some scientists prefer other words. They say that a bacterium responds to substances by fixed chemistry, and that words such as 'decide' and 'talk' belong to animals with brains. Both sides agree on what the bacteria do.
examples: The light-making bacteria in a bobtail squid glow only when they are crowded together in her pouch.
Bacteria in the film on a tooth change their behaviour once the film is thick.
A bacterium in the gut swims towards a sugar and away from an acid.
explanations.art: Many small bacteria in a pouch passing tiny dots to each other, with a light bulb drawn above the whole crowd.

explanations.concept: Animals have always lived among bacteria
explanations.definition: Bacteria and archaea lived on Earth for more than two billion years before the first animals. So no animal has ever lived in a world without microbes.
explanations.description: The oldest signs of life on Earth are about three and a half billion years old, and they are of microbes. The first animals appeared less than one billion years ago, in seas already full of bacteria. By then bacteria had changed the whole planet. The oxygen in the air was first made by bacteria who used sunlight, long before there were plants. Every animal body since then has grown up with bacteria on every surface. In 2013 Margaret McFall-Ngai and many other biologists wrote that this should change how animals are studied. An animal's gut, skin and defences took shape among bacteria. The closest case is inside your own cells. Each cell holds small parts called mitochondria, which release energy from food. They have their own DNA, and it is like the DNA of bacteria. Lynn Margulis argued in 1967 that mitochondria are the descendants of bacteria who came to live inside larger cells about two billion years ago. Her paper was turned down by about fifteen journals before one printed it. The evidence from DNA later showed she was right. So the story of bodies and bacteria living together goes back to the beginning of bodies.
examples: Every cell in your body holds mitochondria, whose ancestors were free-living bacteria.
A cow, a termite and an elephant each depend on gut microbes to break down plants.
A human baby, an elephant calf and a squid hatchling each gather microbes in the first hours and days of life.
explanations.art: A long timeline with bacteria along almost all of it and a small section at the end where animals appear, each animal carrying dots.

explanations.concept: Is the stomach bacterium an enemy or an old companion?
explanations.definition: Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium who lives in the stomach of at least half of all people. She causes ulcers and stomach cancer in some of them. Scientists disagree about whether she also does some good.
explanations.description: Until the 1980s doctors thought no bacterium could live in stomach acid. They blamed stomach ulcers, which are open sores in the stomach wall, on worry and spicy food. In 1982 Robin Warren and Barry Marshall in Australia grew a spiral bacterium from the stomachs of ulcer patients. Few doctors believed them. In 1984 Marshall swallowed a broth of the bacteria. Within days he was vomiting, and a camera showed his stomach lining was inflamed. The two men received the Nobel Prize in 2005. Today ulcers are cured with antibiotics. Yet most carriers never fall ill. A study of the bacterium's genes in 2007 showed that she has travelled with humans since before people left Africa, about 58,000 years ago. She is now disappearing from many countries.
examples: A person with an ulcer who carries the bacterium is treated with antibiotics and is usually cured.
Most people who carry the bacterium never know, because they never fall ill.
In many countries far fewer children carry the bacterium today than their grandparents did as children.

perspectives.who: Barry Marshall, Robin Warren and most stomach doctors
perspectives.explanation: The bacterium causes most stomach ulcers and raises the chance of stomach cancer. A person who is found to carry her and has stomach trouble should be treated. Losing her is a gain for health.

perspectives.who: Martin Blaser, an American doctor and microbiologist
perspectives.explanation: People carried this bacterium for tens of thousands of years, and she changes how the stomach makes acid. In a study of 7,663 American adults in 2007, carriers of one type of the bacterium were less likely to have had asthma. Her disappearance may have costs that we are only beginning to see.

perspectives.who: Scientists who are cautious about both claims
perspectives.explanation: The asthma finding is a link between two things, which is not proof that one causes the other. Children who carry the bacterium may differ in other ways, such as growing up in larger families. More careful studies are needed before anyone is left untreated.

explanations.art: A spiral-shaped bacterium tucked into the mucus layer of a stomach wall, with a question mark above.

agreed.text: Every healthy human carries trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria, and most of them are in the large intestine.
agreed.evidence: In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo worked out the numbers organ by organ. They found about 38 trillion bacteria in a grown-up, nearly all in the large intestine, weighing about 200 grams in total.

agreed.text: Different parts of one body hold different communities, and the place matters more than the person.
agreed.evidence: Grice and Segre's team swabbed 20 skin places on 10 people in 2009. Costello's team compared up to 27 body places on several people over months in the same year. Both read the genes of the bacteria.

agreed.text: Growing microbes on a dish misses most kinds. Reading genes finds many more.
agreed.evidence: In 1999 Kroes, Lepp and Relman found 28 kinds by growing and 59 by reading genes in one sample of tooth film. In 2005 Eckburg's team found that most of the bacteria in the gut belonged to kinds never grown before.

agreed.text: Residents make it harder for harmful microbes to settle.
agreed.evidence: After antibiotics thin the gut residents, Clostridioides difficile can take over. In a trial in the Netherlands in 2013, putting back a healthy person's gut bacteria cured 13 of 16 patients at the first try.

agreed.text: Only a small share of all kinds of microbes can make humans ill.
agreed.evidence: A count in 2001 listed 1,415 kinds of living beings and viruses known to make humans ill, of which 538 were bacteria. More than 500 kinds of microbes live in human mouths alone.

agreed.text: A child's gut community is built in steps over about the first three years.
agreed.evidence: The TEDDY study followed 903 children from 3 to 46 months of age and read the genes in more than 12,000 stool samples. Whether the child was getting mother's milk was the strongest influence found.

agreed.text: People who live together share skin microbes, and dogs add to the sharing.
agreed.evidence: Song's team sampled 60 families in 2013. Household members shared more microbes than people from different homes, most of all on the skin.

challenging.claim: A person and their microbes are one living unit, and should be studied as one.
challenging.who: Biologists who use the word holobiont for a host together with all the microbes living on that host
challenging.for: No animal lives without microbes. Microbes shape how the gut and the defences grow, and some pass from mother to child.
challenging.against: Nancy Moran and Daniel Sloan pointed out in 2015 that most residents are picked up from the surroundings and live for themselves. Microbes in one body also compete with each other.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a body and the microbes living on it count as one being or as many.

challenging.claim: Healthy lungs, bladders and other inner organs are free of microbes.
challenging.who: Medical textbooks for most of the 1900s
challenging.for: Standard ways of growing bacteria found nothing in samples from these organs in healthy people.
challenging.against: Reading genes found small communities in healthy lungs. In 2014 better ways of growing found living bacteria in most urine samples tested, including samples from healthy women.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that only the skin, mouth and gut carry microbes.

challenging.claim: The bacterium Helicobacter pylori may protect some children from asthma.
challenging.who: Martin Blaser and Yu Chen, in a study published in 2007
challenging.for: Among 7,663 adults, those carrying one type of the bacterium were less likely to have had asthma, most of all asthma that began in childhood.
challenging.against: The study found a link, which is not proof of a cause. The bacterium also causes ulcers and stomach cancer, so doctors do not leave her untreated in people who are ill.
challenging.context: This card is about a stomach bacterium who causes illness in some people and may do good in others.

challenging.claim: Antibacterial soap protects a healthy family better than plain soap.
challenging.for: The added chemicals do kill bacteria in laboratory tests.
challenging.against: In 2016 the United States Food and Drug Administration removed 19 such chemicals from home handwashes. Makers had not shown that the products were safe for daily use over many years, or that they worked better than plain soap and water.
challenging.context: This card is about soaps and handwashes with added chemicals that kill bacteria.

challenging.claim: Taking a probiotic after antibiotics helps the gut residents return.
challenging.who: Many doctors and chemists, who suggest probiotic capsules or drinks with antibiotics
challenging.for: Probiotics lower the chance of loose stools during antibiotics in some studies.
challenging.against: In a study at the Weizmann Institute in 2018, people who took a probiotic after antibiotics regained their own gut community more slowly than people who took nothing.
challenging.context: This card is about whether swallowing helpful bacteria speeds up recovery after an antibiotic.

challenging.claim: City life is making our gut communities poorer in kinds.
challenging.who: Justin and Erica Sonnenburg and other scientists who compare people living in different ways
challenging.for: The Hadza people of Tanzania, who hunt and gather their food, carry gut bacteria that have become rare or are missing in people in cities.
challenging.against: Nobody has shown that carrying fewer kinds causes illness. People differ in food, medicines, water and much else at the same time.
challenging.context: This card is about whether modern food and medicines are changing which microbes live in people.

big_questions.q: Trillions of other beings live on you and in you. Is your body a someone, or a place where many someones live?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether one thing can be both. A tree is a living being, and a tree is also a home.

big_questions.q: The same bacterium helps in the gut and harms in the bladder. So is she a good microbe or a bad one?
big_questions.hint: Ask what the word 'bad' is describing: the microbe, the place, or what happens between them.

big_questions.q: Your potato slice showed only the microbes who like potato and air. What else do we miss because of the way we look?
big_questions.hint: Think of other tools: a net with big holes, a torch at night, a question on a form.

big_questions.q: A mother's milk has sugars that feed her baby's bacteria and that the baby cannot digest. Who is the milk for?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether feeding the baby's bacteria is also a way of feeding the baby.

big_questions.q: Most microbes on you seem to do nothing for you. Do they need a reason to be there?
big_questions.hint: Ask the same question about a crow on your building or moss on a wall.

big_questions.q: If a medicine removes a bacterium who has lived with humans for 58,000 years, has something been lost?
big_questions.hint: Weigh the people cured of ulcers against what nobody yet knows.

big_questions.q: Bacteria sense how many neighbours they have and then act together. Is that a decision?
big_questions.hint: Compare what the bacteria do with what a crowd of people does when it starts to clap.

story.title: The Clean Corner
story.note: Madhi, her grandmother Chikki, the calf Thumbi and the old elephant Valli are made up, and so is the camp. How fast the calf gets better is imagined. These facts are real. Forest camps in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu raise orphaned elephant calves by hand. Bomman and Bellie, the carers shown in the film The Elephant Whisperers, belong to the Kattunayakan community. An elephant has no tools of her own for breaking down grass and leaves, and depends on the microbes in her gut. Elephant calves eat the dung of their mothers and other elders. A handbook for people who raise orphaned Asian elephants says this helps a healthy community of microbes to settle in the gut. It tells carers to give calves dung from healthy grown-up elephants.
text: Madhi was eleven the summer she came to live at the elephant camp by the river. Her grandmother Chikki had worked there for thirty years. She had raised four orphan calves, and people said that no calf in her care had ever died.

The fifth calf had come in March. Men cutting bamboo found her beside a dry stream bed, three months old and alone. Nobody knew what had happened to her herd. Chikki named her Thumbi, the dragonfly, because she was never still.
Madhi was given one job. 'Keep her shed clean,' said Chikki. 'A calf without a mother falls ill easily.'

Madhi was good at clean. Every morning she carried out the old straw and laid down new. She scrubbed the milk bottles with ash and hot water and stood them in the sun. She swept the yard in front of the shed until the earth showed the lines of her broom.

Beside Thumbi's shed stood Valli, an old cow elephant who had worked in the forest all her life. Valli dropped her dung where she stood, in great round balls, many times a day. Madhi swept those up too. She was quick about it. No ball lay on the ground long enough to draw a fly.

For a while all went well. Thumbi drank her milk and chased the camp dogs. Then, in her sixth month, Chikki began to give her green food, as a herd would have done. Tender grass came first, then banana stem, then leaves.

Thumbi ate all of it. And all of it came out again, loose and sour, with the blades of grass still green and whole. Her belly swelled tight as a drum. She stood with her head low. In two weeks the bones of her hips began to show.
Chikki changed the grass. She stopped the banana stem. She sat up at night with her hand on the calf's belly. Nothing helped.
Madhi swept harder. Somewhere, she was sure, she had missed some dirt.

One thing made her cross. Whenever Valli dropped a fresh ball, Thumbi stretched her small trunk through the rails towards it. 'Chi! Dirty!' Madhi would say. She would push the trunk back and whisk the ball away. Thumbi would squeal and reach again. It became a race between the trunk and the broom, and the broom always won.

One morning Madhi overslept. When she ran out, the sun was already on the yard. Valli had dropped a ball beside the rails an hour before, and Thumbi had it. She had broken it open with her foot. She was putting the pieces into her mouth one at a time, with great care, in a way she had never eaten her grass.
Madhi's stomach turned. She ran for her grandmother. 'She is eating Valli's dung! I was late. It is my fault. Now she will be worse.'
Chikki came, wiping her hands on her sari. She looked at the calf for a long time. She did not hurry.
'How long has she been asking for it?' she said.
'Asking?'
'Reaching, like that.'
Madhi thought. 'Since she began on grass. Every day. I never let her.'
Chikki sat down on the step slowly, as if something heavy had been put in her lap. 'Thirty years,' she said, 'and I did not see it. My other four were never kept so clean.'
She picked a blade of grass and held it out. 'Can you eat this?'
'No.'

'Nor can she. Nor can Valli. No elephant can break grass down by herself. In Valli's belly live others, too small to see, more of them than there are leaves in this forest. They break the grass, and Valli lives on what they leave over. A calf is born without them. Milk she can manage alone. But grass?' She tapped Madhi's broom with the blade. 'In the forest a calf gets them from her mother's dung, and her aunts' dung. She eats it in the weeks when she starts on leaves. Nobody teaches her. She knows what she is missing.'
Madhi looked at her yard. It was the cleanest yard in the camp. Every morning she had swept away the one thing the calf needed.
'I thought dung was only dirt,' she said.
'To us it is dirt,' said Chikki. 'To her it is seed for an empty field.'

They let Thumbi finish. The camp's animal doctor came and checked Valli's dung, to be sure the old elephant carried no illness. After that Madhi kept one corner by the rails unswept. Each morning she chose a fresh ball from Valli and put it there herself, as carefully as she chose bananas.

It did not happen in a day. For a week nothing changed. Then the sour smell went. Then the swelling went down. One morning in the third week Madhi found Thumbi's dung lying in the straw in firm round balls, small copies of Valli's. She broke one open with a stick. There was no green blade in it anywhere. There were only fine pale threads, worked down by someone to almost nothing.
That evening Chikki fed Madhi her supper by hand, as she had when Madhi was small. She rolled the rice and rasam into a ball with her fingers. Madhi watched the fingers.
'Ajji,' she said, 'who gave me mine?'
Her grandmother put the ball of rice into her mouth. 'Who do you think?' she said.
story.epiphany: The calf was not eating dirt. She was gathering the microbes that every elephant needs to break down grass. The place Madhi kept cleanest was the place that was missing what the calf needed most.
ask: Thumbi's shed was very clean, yet she could not digest grass. What was missing?
Where do you think your own gut microbes came from?
When is cleaning something a help, and when could it take away something that is needed?
art: A girl of eleven sweeping a bare earth yard with a long broom beside a wooden elephant shed, while a small elephant calf stretches her trunk through the rails towards a ball of dung.
An old woman in a sari sitting on a step holding out one blade of grass to a girl, with an old elephant and a calf standing behind them in morning light.

games.title: Which Land? A card game of who lives where on a body
games.context: This is a card game about the habitats of the body. Each card is a clue spoken by a microbe or another tiny being. You say which land of the body they live in, and what about that land suits them.

printables.title: 24 clue cards to cut out (the land is on the back)

items.f: I eat skin oil and I stay away from oxygen. On young children I am hard to find. Where do I live?
items.b: OILY SKIN. Deep in the oil pores of the forehead and nose. I am the bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, and I become common in the teens when skin makes more oil.

items.f: I am an animal with eight legs, too small to see. I eat skin oil. Nearly every grown-up carries me. Where do I live?
items.b: OILY SKIN. In the hair pores of the face. I am a Demodex mite. I am not a microbe, but I am one of the residents.

items.f: I am a yeast. I am the commonest fungus on the head, the body and the arms. Where do I live?
items.b: OILY SKIN. On the scalp, face and body, wherever there is skin oil. I am Malassezia.

items.f: We are a mixed crowd of many kinds, but few of each. Our land has little water and little oil. Where do we live?
items.b: DRY SKIN. On the forearm. Flakes of dead skin fall off all day and carry many of us away.

items.f: My land is thick and dry, and it is washed many times a day. Where do I live?
items.b: DRY SKIN. On the palm of the hand. Residents live deep in the skin there, and visitors come and go.

items.f: I need water. I live where skin folds and sweat stays. Where do I live?
items.b: DAMP SKIN. In the armpit and the elbow crease. I am one of the Corynebacteria.

items.f: I feed on sweat inside a closed shoe and make a cheesy smell. My relatives give strong cheeses their smell. Where do I live?
items.b: DAMP SKIN. On the feet. I am one of the Brevibacteria.

items.f: We are fungi of many kinds. We like warm, damp gaps and thick skin. Where do we live?
items.b: DAMP SKIN. Between the toes and on the heel. Healthy feet carry more kinds of fungi than any other skin.

items.f: I change a substance in a grown-up's sweat into a strong-smelling one. Where do I live?
items.b: DAMP SKIN. In a grown-up's armpit. I am Staphylococcus hominis. A child's armpit does not yet make the substance I use.

items.f: I live in some people's noses. I make a substance that kills a harmful bacterium. Where do I live?
items.b: NOSE. I am Staphylococcus lugdunensis. People who carry me rarely carry Staphylococcus aureus.

items.f: About one person in four carries me without knowing. In a deep wound I am dangerous. Where do I live?
items.b: NOSE. I am Staphylococcus aureus. In the nose I do no harm. In a wound or in the blood I cause serious illness.

items.f: I am long and thin. I stand up from a hard white surface like a spine, and others sit at my tip. Where do I live?
items.b: MOUTH. In the film on a tooth. I am a thread-shaped Corynebacterium, and other bacteria build around me.

items.f: I turn sugar into acid on a hard white surface. Where do I live?
items.b: MOUTH. On a tooth. I am Streptococcus mutans. In a thick film fed with sweets, my acid makes holes.

items.f: I avoid oxygen, so I live deep inside a film, underneath my neighbours. Saliva flows past above me. Where do I live?
items.b: MOUTH. Deep in the film on a tooth, or under the edge of the gum. My neighbours on top use up the oxygen.

items.f: I eat the waste acid that my neighbours make from sugar. I sit right beside them on a hard white surface. Where do I live?
items.b: MOUTH. In the film on a tooth. One community's waste is another's food.

items.f: I burrow into the slippery lining of a very acid place. I make a substance that weakens the acid around me. Where do I live?
items.b: STOMACH. I am Helicobacter pylori. At least half of all people carry me, and most of them never fall ill.

items.f: Oxygen is poison to me. I break down the plant fibre that you cannot digest. Where do I live?
items.b: LARGE INTESTINE. I am one of the fibre-eating bacteria, such as Bacteroides. The gut wall uses what I leave over.

items.f: I am not a bacterium, though I look like one. I use up hydrogen gas and make methane. Where do I live?
items.b: LARGE INTESTINE. I am an archaeon. By using up the hydrogen, I help the fibre-eaters to carry on.

items.f: I eat special sugars in mother's milk that a baby cannot digest. Where do I live?
items.b: LARGE INTESTINE of a baby. I am Bifidobacterium. While the baby drinks only milk, I am often the biggest group there.

items.f: Here I live quietly. If I reach the bladder, I cause a painful infection. Where do I live?
items.b: LARGE INTESTINE. I am Escherichia coli. I am the commonest cause of bladder infections.

items.f: I am tough, and my neighbours keep my numbers small. After a long course of antibiotics I can take over. Where do I live?
items.b: LARGE INTESTINE. I am Clostridioides difficile. When the residents around me are killed, I multiply and cause severe diarrhoea.

items.f: I am a soil bacterium. An hour ago a child repotted a plant. Where am I now?
items.b: JUST VISITING. On the fingers. I am built for soil, and soap and water will rinse me off.

items.f: I lived on a tongue until a minute ago. Then I was swallowed. Where am I now?
items.b: JUST VISITING. In the stomach. The acid will kill me, like most of the bacteria swallowed in saliva.

items.f: I rode in on the family dog's fur and landed on a child's arm. Where am I now?
items.b: JUST VISITING. On dry skin. I may be gone by tomorrow, or I may settle. Scientists cannot yet tell which.

printables.title: A mat with eight spaces
items: OILY SKIN: forehead, nose and scalp. Food: skin oil. Little oxygen deep in the pores.
DRY SKIN: forearm and palm. Little water, little oil.
DAMP SKIN: armpit, elbow crease, toe gaps and feet. Water and salts from sweat.
NOSE: warm, moist air passing through.
MOUTH: teeth, tongue, cheeks and gums. Saliva flows all the time.
LARGE INTESTINE: slow, full of fibre, no oxygen.
JUST VISITING: a microbe from somewhere else, who will not stay long.

rules: Draw the mat with its eight spaces on a sheet of paper. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, clue side up.
On your turn, read the top clue aloud. Say which land the speaker lives in. Say one thing about that land that suits them.
Turn the card over. The land is the first words in capitals. If you named it, keep the card.
If you did not name it, read the back aloud and put the card on that space of the mat.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 16 or more of the 24 cards. Then shuffle the cards from the mat and try those again.

setup.art: A sheet of paper ruled into eight labelled spaces: oily skin, dry skin, damp skin, nose, mouth, stomach, large intestine and just visiting.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the mat with eight spaces.

setup.art: A pile of small cards, clue side up, beside the mat.
setup.caption: 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and pile them clue side up.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud and pointing at one space on the mat.
setup.caption: 3. Read a clue, name the land, then turn the card over.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Draw the mat and read the eight spaces aloud. 3. Shuffle the cards and pile them clue side up.
flow.say: Each card is a clue from someone who lives on a body, or is passing through. There are eight places they could be. Let us read the eight spaces first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw the mat. Read the eight spaces. Mix the cards and make a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Land? Here you set up the clue cards and the mat of eight body habitats.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a clue, name the land and give a reason. 2. Turn the card over and check. 3. Keep the card if you named the land. If not, put it on the mat.
flow.say: Read the clue slowly. What does this one need: water, oil, acid or no oxygen? Which land gives that?
flow.kid: Read the clue. Say which land it is. Say why. Turn the card over and check.
flow.parent: If your child is stuck, ask what the speaker needs and which land gives it. Several mouth cards have the same land for different reasons, and that is part of the idea.
flow.context: In this step of Which Land? you take turns to read a clue and name the body habitat where that microbe lives.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards each player kept. 2. Look at the cards on the mat and read their backs again. 3. Ask which land had the most cards, and why that might be.
flow.say: Which land has the most residents in this game? Why would so many kinds live there?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Read the cards on the mat again. Say which land has the most cards.

ask.q: Three cards were 'just visiting'. What makes someone a visitor and not a resident?
good: They are built for somewhere else, such as soil.
They cannot hold on or find food here.
They are washed off or killed soon.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Land? Here you count the cards and look at which body habitats hold the most kinds.

games.title: Helper, Passenger or Trouble? Find the same microbe in two places
games.context: This is a card game about why the same microbe can be harmless in one place and harmful in another. The 20 cards are ten pairs. Each pair shows one kind of microbe in two situations. You give a verdict for each card, then find the partner card and say what changed.

printables.title: 20 situation cards to cut out, in ten pairs (the verdict is on the back)

items.f: Pair 1. A gut bacterium, Escherichia coli, lives in the large intestine of a healthy child.
items.b: PASSENGER. Most kinds of this bacterium live quietly in the gut and cause no illness.

items.f: Pair 1. The same gut bacterium reaches the bladder.
items.b: TROUBLE. She multiplies there and causes a painful infection. What changed: the place.

items.f: Pair 2. Staphylococcus aureus lives inside the nose of a healthy teacher.
items.b: PASSENGER. About one person in four carries this bacterium in the nose and never knows.

items.f: Pair 2. The same nose bacterium gets into a deep cut.
items.b: TROUBLE. In a wound or in the blood she causes serious illness. What changed: the place.

items.f: Pair 3. Acid-making bacteria live in a thin film on teeth that are brushed twice a day.
items.b: PASSENGER. In a thin film they make too little acid to harm the tooth.

items.f: Pair 3. The same bacteria live in a thick film, and their person sips sweet drinks all day.
items.b: TROUBLE. With plenty of sugar and a thick film, their acid makes holes. What changed: their numbers and their food.

items.f: Pair 4. A few Clostridioides difficile bacteria live in a crowded, healthy gut.
items.b: PASSENGER. The many residents around them keep their numbers small.

items.f: Pair 4. The same bacteria live in a gut after weeks of antibiotics.
items.b: TROUBLE. Their neighbours have been killed, so they multiply and cause severe diarrhoea. What changed: the neighbours.

items.f: Pair 5. A little yeast lives in the mouth, among many bacteria.
items.b: PASSENGER. The bacteria around the yeast leave little room and food.

items.f: Pair 5. The same yeast is in the mouth of someone who has just finished a long course of antibiotics.
items.b: TROUBLE. The yeast multiplies into a sore white coating. What changed: the neighbours.

items.f: Pair 6. A skin bacterium on a forearm makes a substance that kills a harmful bacterium.
items.b: HELPER. Such residents protect the skin. People with eczema have few of them.

items.f: Pair 6. The same kind of skin bacterium grows on a plastic tube that goes into a hospital patient's vein.
items.b: TROUBLE. On the tube she is past the wall of the skin, and she can cause illness. What changed: the place.

items.f: Pair 7. Fibre-eating bacteria live in the large intestine.
items.b: HELPER. They break down fibre, and the cells of the gut wall use what they leave over.

items.f: Pair 7. The same bacteria leak into the belly when an appendix bursts.
items.b: TROUBLE. Outside the gut wall they cause a dangerous infection. What changed: the place.

items.f: Pair 8. Bifidobacterium lives in the gut of a baby who drinks mother's milk.
items.b: HELPER. She eats milk sugars the baby cannot digest, and she is often the biggest group in the baby's gut.

items.f: Pair 8. Curd bacteria are swallowed by a grown-up with a bowl of curd rice.
items.b: PASSENGER. Curd is good food. In many people the swallowed bacteria pass through without settling. What changed: the place and the age.

items.f: Pair 9. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach of a woman who has never had stomach trouble.
items.b: PASSENGER, as far as anyone knows. Most carriers never fall ill.

items.f: Pair 9. The same kind of bacterium lives in the stomach of a man who has an ulcer.
items.b: TROUBLE. She causes most stomach ulcers. Nobody fully knows why she harms some carriers and not others.

items.f: Pair 10. A few fungi live between the toes of healthy feet.
items.b: PASSENGER. Healthy feet carry many kinds of fungi.

items.f: Pair 10. Toe fungi multiply on feet kept damp in closed shoes all day, and the skin itches and peels.
items.b: TROUBLE. In a land that stays wet they grow too many. What changed: the dampness and their numbers.

printables.title: A score sheet for two players
items: Partners found with what changed (1 point each)

rules: Cut out the 20 cards. Spread them on the table, situation side up, in any order.
On your turn, choose a card and read it aloud. Say your verdict: helper, passenger or trouble. Give your reason.
Turn the card over. If your verdict matches the back, you score 1 point.
Now find the partner card with the same pair number. Before you turn it over, say what changed between the two cards: the place, the numbers, the food, the neighbours or the body.
Turn the partner over. If you named what changed, you score 1 more point. Put both cards aside.
A helper does something useful for the body. A passenger lives there and neither helps nor harms, as far as anyone knows. Trouble means illness.
When all ten pairs are gone, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone: try to score 15 or more out of 20.

setup.art: Twenty small cards spread out on a table, situation side up.
setup.caption: 1. Spread out the 20 cards, situation side up.

setup.art: A child holding one card and speaking, with three word bubbles showing a tick, a dash and a cross.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Say helper, passenger or trouble, and why.

setup.art: Two cards with the same pair number side by side, with an arrow between them labelled 'what changed?'.
setup.caption: 3. Find the partner card and say what changed.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and spread them out, situation side up. 2. Explain the three verdicts. 3. Explain that the cards come in pairs.
flow.say: Each card shows a microbe in one situation. Is she a helper, a passenger or trouble? Every microbe appears on two cards.
flow.kid: Spread out the cards. Learn the three verdicts: helper, passenger and trouble. The cards come in pairs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Helper, Passenger or Trouble? Here you set out 20 cards that show ten microbes in two situations each.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Read a card, give a verdict and a reason, and check the back. 2. Find the partner card. Say what changed before you turn it over. 3. Write the points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Give your verdict and your reason. Now find her partner card. It is the same microbe. What is different about where she is?
flow.kid: Read a card. Say your verdict and why. Check the back. Find the partner card. Say what changed.
flow.parent: Children often want every microbe to be good or bad for ever. When a pair surprises them, ask what the microbe herself did differently. Usually nothing: the place, the numbers or the neighbours changed.
flow.context: In this step of Helper, Passenger or Trouble? you judge each situation card and then find the same microbe in a different situation.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points. 2. Ask your child to sort the ten 'what changed' answers into groups. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at the ten pairs again. What kinds of change turned a harmless microbe into trouble? Can you put them into groups?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Sort the ten changes into groups. How many kinds of change did you find?

check.q: In most of the ten pairs, what turned a harmless microbe into trouble?
options: The microbe became a different kind
The person stopped washing
The microbe grew older
The place, the numbers or the neighbours changed
check.why: In every pair the microbe is the same kind on both cards. What differs is where she is, how many there are, or who is around her. Choosing 'the microbe became a different kind' comes from thinking of germs as a fixed group, apart from all other microbes.

flow.context: This is the last step of Helper, Passenger or Trouble? Here you look for a pattern in what turns a harmless microbe into a harmful one.

experiments.title: The Three Lands Test: which part of your skin grows the most spots?
experiments.context: In this experiment you rub clean, wet cotton buds on three places on your own skin: your forearm, your forehead and a gap between your toes. You wipe each bud on a slice of boiled potato in a sealed bag. Over three days you count the spots that grow. You find out whether three places on one skin carry the same microbes.
experiments.question: Your forearm, your forehead and the gap between your toes are all your own skin. Do they carry the same number and the same kinds of microbes who can grow on potato?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which slice will grow the most spots: the forearm slice, the forehead slice or the toe gap slice? Which will grow the fewest? Will the slice that no skin touched stay clear? Write each guess and the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: All four slices come from the same boiled potato and are the same thickness. Each gets one new cotton bud, wetted in the same cooled boiled water. Each place on the skin gets the same ten rubs, and each slice gets the same five lines. All four bags lie side by side in the same warm, dark place. Only one thing differs: the place on the skin that the bud touched. The fourth slice gets a wet bud that touched no skin. It shows what grows from the potato, the water and the air alone.
results_table: What the skin there feels like
Colours and look of the spots

materials.item: a large potato, boiled whole with the skin on for 25 minutes and cooled under a lid
a knife and a plate, rinsed with just-boiled water (for the grown-up)
new clear zip bags (or four clean steel katoris, each covered with a plate)
cotton buds from a new or closed pack
drinking water, boiled and cooled in a covered katori
paper labels and a pen: Forearm, Forehead, Toe gap, No skin
a magnifying glass, or the zoom on a phone camera, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils and cuts the potato. Once the bags are sealed, never open them again, and never sniff them. A spot holds millions of microbes, and growing them makes far more than your skin ever carries. Anyone with asthma should not handle bags with fuzzy mould. At the end a grown-up puts the sealed bags in the dustbin and everyone washes hands with soap. Do not swab a cut, a rash, the inside of the nose or the mouth.

schedule.what: Look at and feel the three places on your skin. Write your guesses and reasons. Swab each place, wipe each bud on its slice, seal the bags and put them in a warm, dark place.
Look through the bags without opening them. Count the spots on each slice and write the numbers down.
Count again. Write down the colours, and whether the spots are shiny, dull or fuzzy.
Count one last time and draw the four slices. Say what you think, what you saw and why. A grown-up throws the sealed bags away. Wash hands.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. On day 4, draw the four slices as four circles, with every spot in its real colour and size. Under the drawing write three sentences. I think: which place carried the most microbes that grow on potato. I saw: the number of spots on each slice. Because: your reason, using what you know about dry, oily and damp skin. If a slice is covered all over, write 'covered' and say what share of the slice is covered.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: spots on each slice on day 4
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your own numbers will be different, and your order may be different too.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a boiled potato with the skin on into four thick slices on a clean steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts four thick slices of boiled potato and seals each in a bag.

setup.art: A child rubbing a wet cotton bud in the gap between two toes.
setup.caption: 2. Rub a new wet cotton bud ten times on one place on your skin.

setup.art: A child's hand drawing a zigzag line with a cotton bud across a potato slice that sits inside an open zip bag.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe the bud in five lines across one slice. Seal the bag.

setup.art: Four sealed zip bags lying flat in a row on a shelf, each with a potato slice and a paper label, and coloured spots on three of the slices.
setup.caption: 4. Keep the bags warm and dark. Count the spots each day without opening.

flow.do: 1. Boil the potato whole for 25 minutes, earlier in the day, and let it cool under a lid. 2. Pour just-boiled water over the knife and the plate. 3. Cut four slices, each as thick as a finger, without touching the cut faces. 4. Slide one slice into each bag and seal the bags at once. 5. Stick on the four labels.
flow.say: I am cutting four slices from one potato. Each slice goes straight into a bag, so that nothing but our swab touches it.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts four thick potato slices. Each slice goes into a bag. Stick a label on each bag.
flow.parent: Boiling kills almost every microbe in the potato, so the slices start nearly empty of life. A few tough resting cells of soil bacteria can survive boiling, which is why one slice is kept as the No skin slice. Cut and bag the slices within an hour of cooling. Thick slices dry out less and grow spots better.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Lands Test. Here a grown-up prepares four slices of boiled potato, the food that the skin microbes will grow on.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to look closely at the forearm, the forehead beside the nose, and the gap between two toes. 2. They press a fingertip on each place and say whether it feels dry, oily or damp. 3. They write one word for each place in the table.
flow.say: Look at these three places on your own skin. Touch each one. How do they feel different? If you were a microbe, which place would you choose to live in?
flow.kid: Look at your forearm, your forehead and a toe gap. Touch each place. Is it dry, oily or damp? Write one word for each.

ask.q: What does a microbe need in order to live and multiply?
good: Water and food.
Warmth and somewhere to hold on.
Some need air and some do not.

flow.parent: Do this at the end of a day, before a bath, when the skin has not been washed for some hours. A child's forehead may not feel oily. That is normal before the teens, and it is worth writing down.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Lands Test you look at and feel three places on your skin, before you swab them.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess for each slice, and a reason for each guess. 2. Ask whether the No skin slice will stay clear. 3. Write the guesses down. Do not say what you expect.
flow.say: Which slice will grow the most spots? Which will grow the fewest? Why do you think so? And what about the slice that no skin touches?
flow.kid: Guess which slice will grow the most spots. Guess which will grow the fewest. Write your reason for each guess.

ask.q: Why do we need a slice that no skin touches?
good: To see what grows without any skin microbes.
So we can compare the others with it.

flow.parent: Every guess is fine if a reason comes with it. Many children guess that the forehead or the toes will win because they seem dirtier. Write the reason down in their words.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Lands Test you guess which place on your skin will grow the most spots on potato, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Start with the No skin bag. Dip a new bud in the cooled boiled water. Open the bag and wipe the bud across the slice in five zigzag lines. Seal the bag and throw the bud away. 2. Dip a new bud. Your child rubs it firmly on the inside of the forearm ten times, turning the bud. Wipe it on the Forearm slice in five lines and seal. 3. Do the same on the forehead beside the nose. 4. Do the toe gap last. 5. Wash hands with soap.
flow.say: A new bud for every place. Ten firm rubs on the skin, then five lines on the slice. Seal each bag before you start the next one.
flow.kid: Dip a new bud in the water. Rub it ten times on your skin. Wipe it in five lines on the slice. Seal the bag. Use a new bud for each place.
flow.parent: The bud must be wet, because a wet bud picks up many more microbes than a dry one. Hold each bag open for as short a time as you can. Rub between the fourth and fifth toes, where the gap is narrowest. If your child has a cut or a rash at one place, use the other arm or foot.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Lands Test you swab three places on your skin and wipe each cotton bud on a different slice of boiled potato.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four bags flat, side by side, slice face up. 2. Put them on a shelf or in a shoebox away from the sun and the stove. 3. Agree on a time to check them every day.
flow.say: The bags stay sealed from now on. We will look through the plastic once a day, at the same time.
flow.kid: Lay the four bags flat in a warm, dark place. Do not open them again. Choose a time to check each day.
flow.parent: At 28 to 32 degrees Celsius, spots usually show within two days. In a cool room they may take four or five days, so go on checking for longer. Sunlight heats the bag and makes water drops that hide the slice.
