flow.wait: Leave the bags sealed in a warm, dark place until tomorrow
flow.context: In this step of the Three Lands Test you put four sealed bags of potato slices in a warm, dark place to grow.

flow.do: 1. On days 2 and 3, look through each bag with the magnifying glass. 2. Count the spots on each slice. 3. Note their colours, and whether they are shiny, dull or fuzzy. 4. Write the numbers in the table. If spots have joined up, write what share of the slice is covered.
flow.say: Count the spots on each slice without opening the bag. What colours do you see? Are the spots on one slice like the spots on another?
flow.kid: Look through each bag. Count the spots on each slice. Write the number and the colours. Never open a bag.

ask.q: Each spot began as one cell or a few cells. How did it become big enough to see?
good: The cell split into two again and again.
They multiplied into millions.

flow.parent: Shiny cream, white and yellow dots are usually bacteria. Fuzzy patches are moulds. The No skin slice often grows one or two spots, or a dull wrinkled film from potato bacteria that survived boiling. Count them anyway, because that slice is what the others are compared with.
flow.wait: Check once a day on day 2 and day 3
flow.context: This step of the Three Lands Test is repeated on day 2 and day 3. You count the spots growing on four potato slices that were wiped with skin swabs.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, count one last time and draw the four slices. 2. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Only then, compare the result with the guesses. 4. Put the sealed bags in the dustbin. Everyone washes hands with soap.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that makes you think so? And why might that place on your skin carry more?
flow.kid: Count one last time and draw the slices. Say what you think, what you saw and why. A grown-up throws the bags away.

ask.q: The forehead slice may have few spots. Does that prove that few microbes live on a forehead?
good: No. It shows only the ones who can grow on potato in air.
No. Some microbes need oil or a place with no oxygen.

ask.q: What would you change to make the test fairer or to learn more?
good: Swab each place twice, on two slices.
Test a grown-up's forehead too.
Swab the same size of skin each time.

flow.parent: The usual result is that the toe gap slice grows the most spots and the forearm slice far fewer. The forehead varies, most of all in children. If your result is different, it is still a result. Ask what might explain it, such as a bath just before, or a bud that was not wet. If every slice is covered with the same wrinkled film, potato bacteria survived the boiling. Boil a fresh potato for longer and try again.

check.q: A slice has only two spots. What does that tell you for certain?
options: Only two microbes lived on that skin
Few microbes who grow on potato in air were on the bud
That skin is cleaner than the rest
The potato was not boiled enough
check.why: A spot grows only from a microbe who can eat potato and live in air. So two spots means few of that kind reached the slice. Choosing 'only two microbes lived there' forgets the many kinds who do not grow on potato.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Three Lands Test. Here you compare four potato slices and explain why three places on one skin gave different results.

experiments.title: Hold the Space: can a newcomer settle in a full gut?
experiments.context: This is a model experiment with a paper grid, rice grains and beans. The grid stands for a patch of gut wall. Rice grains are residents and beans are harmful newcomers. You play the same dice game on a full grid and on a nearly empty one, three times each, and compare how many squares the newcomers win.
experiments.question: A harmful microbe lands in a gut. Does it matter how many residents are already living there?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After eight rounds, how many of the 36 squares will the newcomers hold on the full grid? How many on the nearly empty grid? Write both numbers and the reason for your guess.
experiments.fair_test: Both kinds of game use the same grid, the same dice and the same three rules, for the same eight rounds. Only one thing differs: how many residents are on the grid at the start. Each kind of game is played three times, because dice are chancy and one game can be a fluke.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a grid of 6 rows and 6 columns, each square about 3 cm wide
uncooked rice grains, for residents
rajma or any large bean, for newcomers
dice (or one die rolled twice)
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Draw the grid. Guess. Play three full-gut games and three after-antibiotic games of eight rounds each. Write the scores and compare them.

experiments.record: Write the score of each of the six games in the table. Then work out the average number of newcomers for the three full-gut games and for the three after-antibiotic games. Draw two bars, one for each average. Under the chart write: I think, I saw, because.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: average number of squares held by newcomers after 8 rounds
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your dice will give different numbers.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a hand-drawn grid of six rows and six columns, the rows and columns numbered 1 to 6, with a ruler and pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a grid of 6 rows and 6 columns. Number the rows and the columns.

setup.art: The same grid with one rice grain on every square except the six squares on the slanting line from corner to corner.
setup.caption: 2. Full gut: put a rice grain on every square except the six on the slanting line.

setup.art: The grid with rice grains only on the six squares of the slanting line, and all other squares empty.
setup.caption: 3. After antibiotic: put rice grains only on the six slanting squares.

setup.art: A child's hand rolling two dice beside the grid, with a few red beans placed on empty squares among the rice grains.
setup.caption: 4. Roll two dice to see where each newcomer lands. Play eight rounds.

flow.do: 1. Rule a grid of 6 rows and 6 columns. 2. Number the rows 1 to 6 down the side and the columns 1 to 6 along the top. 3. Count out the rice grains and the beans.
flow.say: This grid is a small patch of gut wall. Each square has room for one microbe. Rice grains are residents. Beans are harmful newcomers.
flow.kid: Draw a grid with 6 rows and 6 columns. Number the rows and columns. Rice grains are residents. Beans are newcomers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hold the Space. Here you draw the grid that stands for a patch of gut wall.

flow.do: 1. Read the three rules of a round aloud, from the rules card below. 2. Explain the two kinds of game. 3. Ask for the two guesses and the reasons. Write them down.
flow.say: A round has three parts. A newcomer arrives. The newcomers multiply. The residents multiply. How many squares will the newcomers hold after eight rounds, in each kind of game? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to the three rules. Guess how many squares the newcomers will win on a full grid. Guess again for a nearly empty grid. Write your reasons.
flow.parent: The rules of a round. One: roll two dice. The first gives the row and the second the column. If that square is empty, put a bean there. If someone is there, the newcomer finds no room and is washed away. Two: every bean that was on the grid before this round adds one new bean on an empty square touching its own by a side, if there is one. Three: the residents add two rice grains, each on an empty square that touches a rice grain by a side.
flow.context: In this step of Hold the Space you learn the three rules of a round. You guess how a newcomer will do on a full grid and on a nearly empty one.

flow.do: 1. Set up the full gut: rice on every square except the six on the slanting line from the top left corner to the bottom right. 2. Play eight rounds. Your child chooses where the two new rice grains go each round. 3. Count the beans, the rice grains and the empty squares. Write them in the table. 4. Clear the grid and play twice more.
flow.say: This gut is full. Thirty residents are at home and six squares are empty. Play eight rounds and count who holds what.
flow.kid: Put rice on all squares except the six slanting ones. Play eight rounds. Count the beans at the end. Play three games.

ask.q: Why did most newcomers find no room?
good: Almost every square already had a resident.
The residents filled the empty squares quickly.

flow.parent: On the full grid a newcomer lands on an empty square only about one time in six at first. The residents fill the gaps within three rounds. Most games end with no beans or one bean.
flow.context: In this step of Hold the Space you play three games on a full grid, which stands for a gut with all its residents.

flow.do: 1. Set up the gut after a long course of antibiotics: rice only on the six slanting squares. 2. Play eight rounds with the same rules. Your child again chooses where the residents multiply. 3. If the grid fills up before round eight, stop and count. 4. Write the numbers in the table. Play twice more.
flow.say: Now an antibiotic has killed most of the residents. Only six are left. The rules are the same. Can you keep the newcomers out this time?
flow.kid: Put rice only on the six slanting squares. Play eight rounds with the same rules. Count the beans. Play three games.

ask.q: You chose where the residents multiplied. Why could you not block the newcomers this time?
good: There were too many empty squares.
The beans multiplied faster than I could block them.

flow.parent: On the nearly empty grid the first bean usually lands in round one or two, and the beans then spread fast. Most games end with 9 to 20 beans. Let your child try hard to block them, because finding that it cannot be done is the point.
flow.context: In this step of Hold the Space you play three games on a nearly empty grid, which stands for a gut after antibiotics have killed most residents.

flow.do: 1. Your child works out the average number of beans for each kind of game. 2. They draw two bars. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason. 4. Then ask what the model leaves out.
flow.say: What do you think now? Which numbers show it? Why does a full grid protect itself? And what does a real gut have that our paper does not?
flow.kid: Work out the average for each kind of game. Draw two bars. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

ask.q: What does a real gut have that this model leaves out?
good: Residents also make substances that harm newcomers.
The body's defence cells.
Food, which residents use up.
Many different kinds of residents.

flow.parent: A model keeps one idea and drops the rest. This one keeps only room. Real residents also use up the food and make substances that stop newcomers, and the gut wall has its own defences. A real course of antibiotics also leaves far more than six residents in every 36.

check.q: In this model, why do newcomers do badly on the full grid?
options: The residents attack them
Almost no square is empty
The dice give them low numbers
The newcomers are weaker
check.why: The rules never let a resident attack. A newcomer simply needs an empty square, and on the full grid there are almost none. Choosing 'the residents attack them' adds something the model does not contain, though real residents do make harmful substances.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hold the Space. Here you compare the scores from the full grid and the nearly empty grid, and say what the model shows.

activities.title: Count the Kinds: how many microbes are germs?
activities.context: In this activity you colour squares to compare three numbers. One is the number of kinds of bacteria known to make people ill. The others are the numbers of kinds that live in human mouths and on healthy skin.

materials.item: squared paper from a maths notebook
colour pencils: red, green and yellow

schedule.what: Colour one square for every 10 kinds: 54 red, 55 green and 100 yellow. Compare the three blocks and say what they show.

activities.record: Keep the coloured sheet. Under the three blocks write one sentence that starts: 'This shows that most microbes ...'.

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper with a small key in the corner showing one square equals ten kinds.
setup.caption: 1. One square stands for 10 kinds of microbes.

setup.art: The squared paper with a block of 54 red squares, a block of 55 green squares and a block of 100 yellow squares side by side.
setup.caption: 2. Colour 54 red, 55 green and 100 yellow squares.

setup.art: A child pointing at the red block and the green block, which are almost the same size.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the blocks. What do you notice?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess. Out of every 100 kinds of microbes, how many can make a person ill? 2. Write the guess at the top of the sheet.
flow.say: Before we count, guess. Out of every hundred kinds of microbes in the world, how many do you think can make a person ill? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Out of 100 kinds of microbes, how many make people ill? Write your guess and your reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Kinds. Here you guess what share of all kinds of microbes can make people ill.

flow.do: 1. Explain that one square stands for 10 kinds. 2. Your child colours 54 squares red, for the 538 kinds of bacteria known in 2001 to make people ill. 3. They colour 55 squares green, for the 553 kinds of microbes known from human mouths. 4. They colour 100 squares yellow, for about 1,000 kinds of bacteria found on healthy skin.
flow.say: Red is every kind of bacterium known to make people ill, anywhere in the world. Green is the kinds living in human mouths. Yellow is the kinds on healthy skin.
flow.kid: One square is 10 kinds. Colour 54 red for germs. Colour 55 green for mouths. Colour 100 yellow for skin.
flow.parent: The red number comes from a count published in 2001, and more have been found since. A few kinds belong to more than one block, because some mouth and skin residents can cause illness in the wrong place.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Kinds you colour squares for germs, for mouth microbes and for skin microbes, to compare the three numbers.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the blocks show. 2. Then say that soil and sea hold far more kinds than all three blocks, and most have no name yet. 3. Your child writes one sentence under the blocks.
flow.say: What do you notice about the red block and the green block? Now think of all the microbes of soil and sea as well. What does that tell you about germs?
flow.kid: Compare the red and green blocks. What do you notice? Write one sentence about what this shows.

ask.q: What do the three blocks tell you?
good: One healthy mouth has about as many kinds as all the germ bacteria in the world.
Germs are a small share of all microbes.

check.q: Which sentence fits the three coloured blocks?
options: Germs are a small share of all kinds of microbes
Most kinds of microbes make people ill
Mouths have no harmless microbes
Skin has fewer kinds than there are germs
check.why: The mouth alone holds about as many kinds as the whole list of germ bacteria, and soil and sea hold far more. Choosing 'most kinds make people ill' is a common idea, because germs are the microbes we hear about most.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Kinds. Here you compare the block of germs with the blocks of harmless mouth and skin microbes.

activities.title: New Land: a strip story of a baby's first three years of microbes
activities.context: In this activity you fold a paper strip into six boxes. You draw how the community of microbes in a baby's gut changes, from the day of birth to the age of three. Then you ask a grown-up three questions about your own first foods.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, made by cutting a sheet in half lengthways and joining the two halves
pencils and colour pencils
a grown-up who knew you as a baby

schedule.what: Fold the strip into six boxes. Draw one stage of a baby's microbes in each box. Ask a grown-up about your own first foods and add them.

activities.record: Keep the strip. In each box, the number of different colours of dots shows how many kinds of microbes there are. Write your own first solid food, and your age then, under box 4.

setup.art: A long paper strip folded into six equal boxes, numbered 1 to 6.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a long strip into six boxes.

setup.art: The strip with a baby drawn in each box, growing older from left to right, and more colours of dots in the belly each time.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the baby and the microbes at each stage.

setup.art: A child asking a grandmother a question and writing the answer under one of the boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Ask a grown-up about your own first foods.

flow.do: 1. Make the strip and fold it into six boxes. 2. Label them: before birth, the day of birth, milk only, first solid food, age one to two, age three. 3. Ask your child to guess in which box the baby first has microbes.
flow.say: A baby is new land for microbes. When do you think the first ones arrive? Where do they come from? Tell me your guess before we draw.
flow.kid: Fold the strip into six boxes. Write a label on each. Guess when a baby gets her first microbes.
flow.context: This is the first step of New Land. Here you make a strip of six boxes for six stages of a baby's first three years.

flow.do: 1. Read the six notes in the parent note aloud, one at a time. 2. After each one, your child draws the baby and colours dots for the microbes. 3. More colours of dots means more kinds.
flow.say: I will read what scientists found for each stage. Draw the baby, then draw the microbes as dots. Use a new colour for each new kind.
flow.kid: Listen to each note. Draw the baby in the box. Colour dots for the microbes. Use more colours for more kinds.
flow.parent: Box 1, before birth: most scientists think a healthy womb has no microbes, so draw no dots. Box 2, the day of birth: the first microbes come from the mother and from the people and things that touch the baby. The same few kinds are all over the body. Box 3, milk only: mother's milk holds sugars that the baby cannot digest. They feed bacteria called Bifidobacterium, who often become the biggest group. Box 4, first solid food: fibre arrives, and fibre-eating kinds settle. Box 5, age one to two: many new kinds arrive from food, people, pets and the floor. Box 6, age three: the community is steady and looks like a grown-up's.
flow.context: In this step of New Land you draw what scientists have found about a baby's microbes at six stages.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks a grown-up three questions. What was my first solid food? How old was I? Who and what did I touch most as a baby? 2. They write the answers under boxes 4 and 5. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Now find out about yourself. Ask what you ate first, how old you were, and who held you most.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up three questions about when you were a baby. Write the answers under your strip.
flow.parent: Babies are born and fed in different ways, and they grow up healthy in all of them. If your child asks, say that plainly. The differences that scientists find between babies become smaller as the children grow.

check.q: Why does the number of kinds of gut microbes rise when a baby starts solid food?
options: Solid food is dirty
The baby's stomach stops making acid
Milk kills microbes
New foods feed new kinds of microbes
check.why: Each kind of microbe needs particular food. Fibre from rice, dal, fruit and vegetables feeds kinds that milk did not. Choosing 'solid food is dirty' treats every microbe as dirt, when these are the residents a child needs.

flow.context: This is the last step of New Land. Here you ask a grown-up about your own first foods and add the answers to your strip.

activities.title: Who Shares My Microbes? A web of my household
activities.context: People who live together share skin microbes with each other and with their pets. In this activity you draw a web of everyone and everything you touch often, and work out where most of your shared microbes pass.

materials.item: a sheet of paper
a pencil and two colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw yourself in the middle of a page. Add the people, animals and things you touch every day. Draw thick lines for the most touching.

activities.record: Keep the web. Circle the three thickest lines. Write one sentence on who you think shares the most skin microbes with you, and why.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a small drawing of a child in the middle, labelled Me.
setup.caption: 1. Draw yourself in the middle.

setup.art: The same sheet with drawings around the child: a mother, a brother, a grandmother, a dog, a sofa, a towel and a school friend.
setup.caption: 2. Add the people, animals and things you touch each day.

setup.art: The web with thick lines to some drawings and thin lines to others.
setup.caption: 3. Thick lines for lots of touching, thin lines for a little.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws themself in the middle of the page. 2. Around the edge they draw everyone who lives in the home, and any pets. 3. They add three things many people touch, such as a sofa, a towel or a phone.
flow.say: Draw yourself in the middle. Now add everyone who lives here, and any animals. Then add three things that many of us touch.
flow.kid: Draw yourself in the middle. Draw the people and pets in your home around you. Add three things that everyone touches.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Shares My Microbes? Here you draw yourself, your household and the things you all touch.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a line from themself to each drawing. 2. A thick line means touching many times a day. A thin line means once a day or less. 3. They add one friend or relative from another home, with the line they think fits.
flow.say: How often do you touch each one? Draw a thick line for many times a day, and a thin line for a little.
flow.kid: Draw a line to each one. Make the line thick for lots of touching. Make it thin for a little.
flow.context: In this step of Who Shares My Microbes? you draw thick and thin lines to show how often you touch each person, pet and thing.

flow.do: 1. Ask who probably shares the most skin microbes with your child, and why. 2. Then tell them what the 2013 study of 60 families found. 3. Your child writes one sentence under the web.
flow.say: Who do you think shares the most skin microbes with you? Why? Scientists tested 60 families. Shall I tell you what they found?
flow.kid: Say who shares the most skin microbes with you. Give your reason. Then hear what scientists found in 60 families.
flow.parent: The study found that people in one home shared more microbes than people from different homes, most of all on the skin. Grown-ups with a dog shared more skin microbes with each other, and with their own dog more than with other dogs. Sharing harmless microbes is ordinary and not a reason to stop touching anyone.

ask.q: Why would the skin show more sharing than the gut?
good: Skin touches people and things directly.
Gut microbes are inside and are harder to pass on.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Shares My Microbes? Here you use your web to work out who shares the most skin microbes with you.

activities.title: The 99.9 Percent Label: what does a handwash really promise?
activities.context: Many soaps and handwashes say they kill 99.9 percent of germs. In this activity you read the labels in your own home and ask what the claim leaves out.

materials.item: soaps, handwashes and cleaners from your home, closed
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Keep every bottle closed. Floor and toilet cleaners are strong chemicals, so a grown-up holds those while you read the label.

schedule.what: Read the labels of three or four soaps and cleaners. Write down each claim. Ask three questions about each claim.

activities.record: Draw a table with four columns: the product, what the label promises, what the small print says, and my question. Fill in one row for each product.

setup.art: A child at a bathroom shelf holding a closed handwash bottle and reading the front label.
setup.caption: 1. Find the promise on the front of the label.

setup.art: A close view of the back of a bottle with a magnifying glass over the small print.
setup.caption: 2. Read the small print on the back.

setup.art: A notebook page with a four-column table and a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Write the promise, the small print and your question.

flow.do: 1. Collect three or four soaps, handwashes and cleaners. Keep them closed. 2. Your child reads the front of each and writes down any promise about germs.
flow.say: Read the front of each one. Does it promise anything about germs? Write down the exact words.
flow.kid: Read the front of each bottle. Find any promise about germs. Write the exact words.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 99.9 Percent Label. Here you find what soaps and cleaners in your home promise about germs.

flow.do: 1. Help your child find the small print for each promise, often beside a star mark. 2. They write what it says. 3. Ask the three questions in the parent note.
flow.say: Now find the small print. Where was this tested? On skin, or in a dish? And on which germs?
flow.kid: Find the small print on the back. Write what it says. Ask where the test was done.
flow.parent: Three good questions. Was the test done on real hands or in a laboratory dish? Which germs were tested, out of the many kinds there are? And does the label say what happens to the harmless residents of the skin? Most labels answer none of these.
flow.context: In this step of the 99.9 Percent Label you read the small print behind a promise about killing germs.

flow.do: 1. Ask what plain soap does. 2. Tell your child about the ruling of 2016 in the parent note. 3. They write one question they would ask the maker.
flow.say: What does plain soap do to the visitors on your hands? Do you think a home needs more than that? Why?
flow.kid: Say what plain soap does. Decide whether a home needs more. Write one question for the maker.
flow.parent: Plain soap does not need to kill anything. It lifts visitors off the skin so that water carries them away. In 2016 the United States Food and Drug Administration removed 19 germ-killing chemicals from home handwashes. The makers had not shown that such washes work better than plain soap and water. Hospitals are different, and so is cleaning a wound.

check.q: Why is plain soap enough for washing hands at home?
options: It kills every microbe on the skin
Homes have no germs
It lifts visitors off so water carries them away
Residents eat the germs
check.why: Soap loosens dirt and the visitors sitting on the skin, and water rinses them off. Choosing 'it kills every microbe' mixes up removing with killing. The residents deep in the pores stay, and that is fine.

flow.context: This is the last step of the 99.9 Percent Label. Here you compare a germ-killing promise with what plain soap already does.

activities.title: The Sniff Test: does fresh sweat smell?
activities.context: People say that sweat smells. In this activity you smell fresh sweat straight after exercise, and then things that were sweaty hours ago. You find out where the smell really comes from.

materials.item: a skipping rope, or room to jump on the spot
socks or shoes that someone has worn all day
a grown-up's shirt worn for a whole warm day

schedule.what: Guess. Skip until you sweat and smell your forearm. In the evening, smell socks worn all day and the underarm of a grown-up's worn shirt. Compare.

activities.record: Write three lines: fresh sweat on my arm smelled of ___, the socks smelled of ___, the shirt smelled of ___. Then write where you think the smell comes from.

setup.art: A child skipping with a rope on a balcony, with small drops of sweat on the forehead.
setup.caption: 1. Skip or jump until you sweat.

setup.art: The child sniffing her own sweaty forearm with a puzzled look.
setup.caption: 2. Smell the fresh sweat on your forearm.

setup.art: In the evening, the child holding a worn sock at arm's length and wrinkling her nose.
setup.caption: 3. In the evening, smell socks worn all day.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child whether fresh sweat smells, and why they think so. 2. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Does sweat smell when it has just come out of your skin? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Does fresh sweat smell? Write your guess and your reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sniff Test. Here you guess whether sweat smells when it is fresh.

flow.do: 1. Your child skips or jumps for three or four minutes, until the forehead and arms are damp. 2. They smell the sweat on their own forearm at once. 3. They write what they smell.
flow.say: Skip until you are sweating. Now smell your forearm straight away. What do you smell?
flow.kid: Skip for three or four minutes. Smell the sweat on your forearm at once. Write what you smell.
flow.parent: Fresh sweat on a forearm is water and salt and has almost no smell. Most children are surprised.
flow.context: In this step of the Sniff Test you make fresh sweat by skipping and smell it straight away.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, your child smells socks or shoes worn all day, from arm's length first. 2. They smell the underarm of a grown-up's shirt worn all day. 3. Ask what is different from the fresh sweat, and what could have made the smell.
flow.say: These were sweaty hours ago. How do they smell now? The sweat had no smell this afternoon. So what changed in between?
flow.kid: In the evening, smell socks worn all day. Smell a grown-up's worn shirt. What changed since the sweat was fresh?

ask.q: The sweat had no smell at first. What made the smell?
good: Bacteria on the skin changed the sweat.
Microbes had hours to multiply in the damp sock.

flow.parent: Skin bacteria feed on substances in sweat and give off smelly ones. That takes time and a damp, closed place, such as a shoe. A grown-up's underarm makes a kind of sweat that a child's does not make until the teens, which is why a child's shirt smells much less.

check.q: Where does the smell of old socks come from?
options: Bacteria change substances in sweat
Sweat always smells
The cloth of the sock
Dirt from the floor
check.why: Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Bacteria living in the damp sock feed on the sweat and give off smelly substances. Choosing 'sweat always smells' is the usual idea, and your own nose just tested it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Sniff Test. Here you smell things that were sweaty hours ago and work out where the smell comes from.

projects.title: My Body Atlas: a book of the lands on me and who lives there
projects.context: In this four-day project you make a small atlas of your own body. An atlas is a book of maps. Yours has a map of the lands of your body, a page for each land and its residents, and a page on how your microbes reached you.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, folded in half and stapled into a book of eight pages
pencils and colour pencils
your results from the Three Lands Test, if you did it
the cards from Which Land?, if you made them

schedule.what: Make the book. On pages 2 and 3, draw a map of your body with its seven lands in different colours, and a key.
Pages 4 and 5: the three skin lands. For each, write what it gives a microbe and who lives there. Add your own test results.
Pages 6 and 7: the mouth and the food tube, from the acid stomach to the crowded large intestine.
Page 8: how my microbes reached me and who I share them with. Draw the cover. Show the atlas to someone at home.

projects.record: The finished atlas is the record. Each land page has three things: what the land gives a microbe (water, oil, acid, air or no air), who lives there, and one thing scientists do not know yet.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper folded in half and stapled along the fold to make a small book.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and staple two sheets into a book of eight pages.

setup.art: An open book showing a child's body outline coloured as a map, with a colour key at the side.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a map of the lands of your body, with a key.

setup.art: An open page headed Damp Skin with small drawings of residents and a table of test results.
setup.caption: 3. Give each land a page: what it offers and who lives there.

setup.art: A child showing the finished small book to a grandmother.
setup.caption: 4. Add how your microbes reached you. Show your atlas to someone.

flow.do: 1. Help your child fold and staple the book. 2. On pages 2 and 3 they draw their body outline. 3. They colour seven lands: oily skin, dry skin, damp skin, nose, mouth, stomach and large intestine. 4. They add a key.
flow.say: An atlas starts with a map of the whole country. Draw your body and colour its lands. What will your key say about each colour?
flow.kid: Make your book. Draw your body on pages 2 and 3. Colour the seven lands. Add a key.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Body Atlas. Here you make the book and draw the map of the lands of your own body.

flow.do: 1. Your child gives the three skin lands a section each on pages 4 and 5. 2. For each they write what the land gives a microbe and who lives there. 3. They add their own spot counts from the Three Lands Test.
flow.say: For each skin land, write what a microbe finds there, and who lives there. Then add what your own test showed.
flow.kid: Write about the three skin lands. Say what each land gives a microbe. Add your own spot counts.
flow.parent: If you did not do the test, your child can use the clue cards from Which Land? in its place.
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Body Atlas. Here you write the pages for the oily, dry and damp lands of your skin.

flow.do: 1. On page 6 your child draws the mouth with its surfaces: teeth, tongue, cheeks and gum edge. 2. On page 7 they draw the food tube. 3. They show the numbers with dots: few in the stomach, crowds in the large intestine.
flow.say: Now the wet lands inside. How will you show that the stomach has very few and the large intestine has the most?
flow.kid: Draw the mouth on page 6. Draw the food tube on page 7. Use few dots for the stomach and many for the large intestine.

ask.q: Why are there so few microbes in the stomach?
good: The acid kills most of them.
Only a few kinds can live in acid.

flow.context: This is day 3 of My Body Atlas. Here you draw the mouth and the food tube, and show where microbes are few and where they are many.

flow.do: 1. On page 8 your child writes how their microbes reached them and who shares them. 2. They add one question that nobody can answer yet. 3. They draw the cover and show the atlas to someone at home.
flow.say: Last page. Where did your residents come from? Who shares them with you now? And what does nobody know yet?
flow.kid: Write how your microbes reached you. Add one question nobody can answer. Draw the cover. Show your atlas.

ask.q: What is one thing in your atlas that scientists are still unsure about?
good: Whether shared skin microbes settle or only pass.
What most residents do for us, if anything.
Whether the stomach bacterium does any good.

flow.context: This is day 4 of My Body Atlas. Here you finish the atlas with a page on where your microbes came from, and show it to someone.

challenges.title: Test the Claim: design a fair test for a germ-killing handwash
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about evidence. A handwash bottle says it kills 99.9 percent of germs. You design a fair test that could show whether it does more for real hands than plain soap.
challenges.problem: A handwash says on the bottle that it kills 99.9 percent of germs. A bar of plain soap costs much less. Design a test that a family could run at home to compare the two on real hands. Your test must be fair, and you must say what it can show and what it cannot.
constraints: Only things found at home: boiled potato slices in sealed bags, cotton buds, cooled boiled water, the handwash and plain soap.
At least one slice must show what unwashed hands carry, and one must show what grows with no hand at all.
Everything except the kind of wash must stay the same.
Each wash is tested on more than one hand or more than one day.
Sealed bags are never opened, and a grown-up throws them away.
materials: your notes from the Three Lands Test
a handwash bottle and a bar of soap, to read the labels
general: Swab the hands before washing and after washing, and compare the two slices.
Wash for the same time, such as 20 seconds, with the same amount of water each time.
Use the same person's left and right hands for the two washes, then swap on another day.
Count spots on the same day for every slice.
creative: Get someone else to label the bags with secret letters, so that the person counting does not know which wash was used.
Add a third wash with water alone, to see how much the rubbing and rinsing do.
Swab again two hours after washing, to see how soon the hands are settled again.
Ask what the test misses: it counts only microbes who grow on potato, and it cannot tell a germ from a harmless resident.
challenges.your_turn: Write your plan as a numbered list, with a drawing of the bags and their labels. Under it, write one sentence on what your test can show and one on what it cannot show. If a grown-up agrees, run the test with the Three Lands method and count the spots after three days.

setup.art: A handwash bottle with a large '99.9%' on the label beside a plain bar of soap on a steel dish.
setup.caption: 1. The problem: is the handwash better for real hands than plain soap?

setup.art: A child drawing a plan with rows of small bags labelled unwashed, plain soap, handwash and no hand.
setup.caption: 2. Plan the slices: which hand, which wash, and what to compare with.

setup.art: A notebook page with a numbered plan and two sentences at the bottom headed 'can show' and 'cannot show'.
setup.caption: 3. Write what your test can show and what it cannot.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child what they would compare, and what must stay the same. 3. Let them list every slice they would need.
flow.say: What two things are we comparing? What else do we need a slice for, so that we can trust the answer?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Say what you would compare. List every slice you need.

ask.q: Why do you need a slice from unwashed hands?
good: To know what was there before washing.
Without it we cannot tell how much each wash removed.

flow.context: This is the first step of Test the Claim. Here you decide what to compare in a test of a germ-killing handwash against plain soap.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes the plan as numbered steps and draws the labelled bags. 2. Check the plan against the five rules. 3. Ask how they will stop one lucky result from fooling them.
flow.say: Write your steps in order. Then check each rule. How will you make sure one odd result does not fool you?
flow.kid: Write your plan in numbered steps. Draw the bags and labels. Check the five rules.
flow.parent: A good plan has at least four kinds of slice: no hand, unwashed, plain soap and handwash. It repeats each wash at least twice. Many children forget that the two hands, or two days, may differ to begin with.
flow.context: In this step of Test the Claim you write a step-by-step plan for a fair test of two ways of washing hands.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual and the creative ideas together. 2. Your child adds one idea to their plan. 3. They write what the test can show and what it cannot.
flow.say: Here are ideas that other testers use. Which one would make your test stronger? And what can your test never tell you?
flow.kid: Read the ideas. Add one to your plan. Write what your test can show and what it cannot.

ask.q: Suppose the handwash slice has fewer spots. Does that prove it keeps a family healthier?
good: No. Fewer spots is not the same as fewer illnesses.
No. The spots may be harmless residents.

flow.context: This is the last step of Test the Claim. Here you improve your plan and write down the limits of your test.

challenges.title: The Careful Medicine: stop one germ and spare the residents
challenges.context: This is an invention challenge on paper. An antibiotic kills a harmful bacterium, and many harmless residents as well. You design a treatment that stops one germ and harms the residents as little as possible.
challenges.problem: A child has an infection caused by one kind of harmful bacterium. The usual antibiotic tablet will cure the infection. It will also kill about a third of the kinds of bacteria in the gut for some weeks. Invent a treatment that stops the one germ and spares as many residents as possible. Draw your idea and explain how it finds or reaches only the germ.
constraints: The infection must still be cured. A treatment that spares the residents but leaves the child ill does not count.
Say how your treatment tells the germ from the residents, or how it reaches only the place where the germ is.
Say one way your treatment could go wrong.
This is a design on paper. Real medicines are chosen by a doctor.
general: Test first to find out which germ is causing the illness, so that the doctor can choose a medicine that works on few kinds of bacteria.
Put the medicine only where the germ is, such as a cream on the skin or drops in the ear, so that less reaches the gut.
Give the medicine for only as long as the doctor finds is needed.
Use no antibiotic at all when the illness is caused by a virus, such as a cold.
creative: Use a virus that attacks only one kind of bacterium. Such viruses are called bacteriophages, and doctors in some countries use them.
Use a substance made by the residents themselves. A nose bacterium makes one that kills Staphylococcus aureus.
Put helpful residents back. In one study, doctors put protective skin bacteria on the skin of people with eczema, and the harmful bacteria became fewer.
Before the medicine, store a sample of the person's own gut bacteria and give it back afterwards. In a study in 2018 this brought the community back within days.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your treatment. Label how it finds the germ, how it reaches the germ, and what it leaves alone. Write two sentences: why the residents are worth sparing, and one way your idea might fail.

setup.art: A drawing of a gut crowded with many colours of dots, with one red dot circled.
setup.caption: 1. The problem: stop the one red germ and spare the rest.

setup.art: A child sketching an invention on paper: a tiny carrier with a label reading 'only fits the red one'.
setup.caption: 2. Draw how your treatment finds or reaches only the germ.

setup.art: A finished labelled drawing with two written sentences underneath.
setup.caption: 3. Label it. Say why the residents matter and how your idea could fail.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask why killing the residents matters. 3. Ask how a medicine could tell one bacterium from another.
flow.say: The tablet cures the child, so what is the problem with it? How could a treatment tell the germ from everyone else?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Say why the residents matter. Think how a medicine could find only the germ.

ask.q: What can go wrong when many gut residents are killed?
good: A tough bacterium can take over the empty space.
Loose stools.
Some kinds may not come back.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Careful Medicine. Here you work out why an ordinary antibiotic harms the residents as well as the germ.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws their treatment. 2. They label how it finds the germ, how it reaches the germ, and what it leaves alone. 3. Do not show the idea lists yet.
flow.say: Draw your own idea first. How does it find the germ? How does it get there? What does it leave alone?
flow.kid: Draw your treatment. Label how it finds the germ. Label what it leaves alone.
flow.parent: Any idea with a reason is welcome, however unusual. Good ideas use a difference between the germ and the residents: a shape, a food, a place or an enemy.
flow.context: In this step of the Careful Medicine you draw your own invention for stopping one germ without harming the residents.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual and the creative ideas aloud. 2. Your child marks any that are like theirs. 3. They write why the residents are worth sparing, and one way their idea could fail.
flow.say: Real scientists are trying these ideas now. Is any of them like yours? What is one way your idea might fail?
flow.kid: Listen to the real ideas. Is one like yours? Write one way your idea might fail.
flow.parent: Say plainly that antibiotics save lives, and that a medicine a doctor has prescribed must be taken as the doctor says. This challenge is about making good medicines better.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Careful Medicine. Here you compare your invention with what scientists are trying, and name a weakness in your own idea.

worksheets.title: Who lives where on a body

items.p: What is a resident microbe?
opts: One who washes off with soap
One who lives and multiplies on a body
items.why: A resident lives and multiplies on or in a body for months or years. Most residents cause no illness, and soap does not remove those deep in the pores.

items.p: A microbe who lands on your skin and is gone within hours is called a ____.
items.why: A visitor comes from soil, food, a handle or another person, and does not stay. Hand washing is aimed at visitors.

items.p: Sort these places by the kind of skin they have.
items.why: The forearm and palm have little water or oil. The forehead and nose have many oil glands. The armpit and toe gaps stay damp with sweat.

items.p: Your forearm and your toe gap carry the same community of microbes.
items.why: False. The forearm is dry and the toe gap is damp, and each suits different microbes. The place on the body decides the community more than the person does.

items.p: Match each land of the body to what it gives a microbe.
items.why: Each land offers different food, water and air. That is why each holds a different community.

items.p: Where do most of a body's bacteria live?
items.why: Nearly all of a grown-up's 38 trillion bacteria are in the large intestine, which is warm, wet, slow and full of fibre. Healthy blood has none. Choosing the skin is common, because skin is the part we see.

items.p: Put these in order, from the fewest bacteria to the most.
items: A millilitre of large intestine contents
a: A millilitre of large intestine contents
items.why: Healthy blood has none. Stomach contents hold a few thousand, because of the acid. Saliva holds about a billion. Large intestine contents hold about a hundred billion.

items.p: A potato slice with no spots proves that the swabbed skin had no microbes.
items.why: False. A spot grows only from a microbe who can eat potato and live in air. Many skin residents need oil, or a place without oxygen, and never show up.

items.p: In the Three Lands Test, why is one slice wiped with a bud that touched no skin?
opts: To show what grows without skin microbes
To use up the spare slice
To keep the other slices clean
items.why: That slice shows what comes from the potato, the water and the air alone. The other slices are compared with it. Without it, you could not tell which spots came from skin.

items.p: Washing hands with soap at home mostly removes which microbes?
items.why: Soap lifts off the visitors on the surface, among whom germs are found. The residents in the pores stay and spread back within hours.

items.p: The oil that skin makes beside each hair is called ____.
items.why: Sebum keeps skin soft, and it is food for the oil-eating bacteria and yeasts of the face and scalp.

items.p: Explain why few bacteria live in the stomach but very many live in the large intestine.
items.a: The stomach is very acid, and the acid kills most bacteria that are swallowed. The large intestine is not acid. It is warm, wet and slow, and it is full of plant fibre for bacteria to eat.
items.why: A strong answer names what each place is like for a microbe: acid in one, food and time in the other.

items.p: In the Three Lands Test, why must every cotton bud get the same ten rubs?
items.a: So that the only thing that differs between the slices is the place on the skin. If one bud got more rubs, more microbes might be picked up there, and the test would not be fair.
items.why: A strong answer says that only one thing may differ in a fair test, and names that thing.

items.p: Draw an outline of a body. Colour the oily, dry and damp skin in three colours, and add a key.
items.a: Oily: forehead, nose, scalp, upper back. Damp: armpits, elbow creases, backs of the knees, toe gaps. Dry: forearms, palms, shins.
items.why: A strong drawing has a key and puts at least two places in each colour.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body, front view.

items.p: Are the microbes on your skin part of you?

views.says: Yes. They have lived on me since I was born, and some of them protect my skin. I would be less healthy without them.
No. They are separate living beings with their own genes. They live on you for their own sake, and many would live on anyone.
It depends on where they are. On your skin they are neighbours. In a deep cut, the same ones are a danger to you.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. The girl is right that some residents protect the skin. The biologist is right that they are separate beings. The doctor is right that the place matters.
items.why: Each view is true from where it stands. A strong answer says what 'part of you' means before deciding.

worksheets.title: Holding the space, and how microbes arrive

items.p: What does 'holding the space' mean?
opts: Residents hold on to the skin
The body keeps microbes out of blood
Residents leave newcomers no room or food
items.why: Residents already cover the surface and eat the food, and some make substances that stop newcomers. So a harmful microbe who arrives finds it hard to settle.

items.p: In Hold the Space, why do newcomers win many squares after the antibiotic?
items.why: The rules and the dice stay the same. Only the number of residents at the start differs, and empty squares are what a newcomer needs.

items.p: An antibiotic kills only the harmful bacteria.
items.why: False. An antibiotic cannot tell a germ from a resident. In one study, five days of an antibiotic made about a third of the kinds of gut bacteria rarer.

items.p: An antibiotic cures a cold.
items.why: False. A cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses. Taking one for a cold harms the residents and leaves the virus alone.

items.p: Put these stages of a baby's gut in order, from first to last.
items: A steady community at about three years
Milk-sugar eaters become the biggest group
The same few kinds all over at birth
a: The same few kinds all over at birth
Milk-sugar eaters become the biggest group
A steady community at about three years
items.why: The gut is settled in steps. Each new food feeds new kinds, and the community becomes steady at about three years.

items.p: Match each thing to what scientists found.
pairs: One hour sitting in a room
Over a million particles given off
Sugars that feed a baby's bacteria
items.why: Microbes pass between bodies by touch, through the air and with food. Each of these was measured in a real study.

items.p: Three of these are ways residents keep newcomers out. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Residents use the food, cover the surface and make substances that stop newcomers. Microbes do not make skin thicker.

items.p: In one game of Hold the Space, newcomers hold 18 of the 36 squares. What percent is that?
items.why: 18 is half of 36, and one half is 50 percent.

items.p: The step-by-step change of a community in a new place is called ____.
items.why: Succession happens on bare rock, in a new pond and in a newborn's gut. The first settlers are joined and replaced by others.

items.p: Sort these microbes into visitors and residents.
items: Soil bacteria on fingers after repotting
Mouth bacteria just swallowed into the stomach
Bacteria picked up from a door handle
items.why: A resident is in a place that suits her and stays there. A visitor is built for somewhere else, or is in a place that will soon kill or remove her.

items.p: A child takes an antibiotic for five days. Explain what happens to the gut residents during the medicine and after it.
items.a: During the medicine, many kinds of gut bacteria are killed or become rare. After it ends, most of them multiply again, and the community is close to how it was within about four weeks. A few kinds may take much longer to return.
items.why: A strong answer has both parts: the loss during the medicine and the return afterwards.

items.p: Hold the Space is a model. Name two things a real gut has that the model leaves out.
items.a: Any two of these. Real residents use up the food. They make substances that stop newcomers. The body has defence cells. A real gut holds hundreds of kinds of residents, not one.
items.why: A strong answer shows that a model keeps one idea and drops others. This model keeps only room.

items.p: Label these four stages of a baby's gut with what the microbes are doing.
a: The day of birth: the first few kinds arrive from the mother and other people
Milk only: milk-sugar eaters are often the biggest group
First solid food: fibre-eaters and many new kinds settle
Age three: the community is steady, like a grown-up's
items.why: Each stage follows from a change in food and in what the child touches.
items.art: A strip of four blank panels showing a newborn, a baby drinking milk, a baby eating rice and a three-year-old.

items.p: A healthy child has a cold. Should she take an antibiotic 'to be safe'?

views.says: Yes. It is better to kill the germs early, before she gets worse.
No. A cold is caused by a virus. The antibiotic would not touch the virus, and it would kill many of her gut residents.
Wait and watch. Give her rest and fluids. If the fever lasts or she gets worse, take her to the doctor.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: The doctor is right about the science: antibiotics do not work on viruses, and they harm residents. The grandmother's plan is sensible care. The uncle's wish to protect the child is kind, but the medicine would not do what he hopes.
items.why: A strong answer separates the wish to help from whether the medicine can help.

items.p: Why does mother's milk hold sugars that a baby cannot digest?
opts: They feed the baby's gut bacteria
items.why: The sugars pass through the baby's stomach untouched and feed Bifidobacterium in the gut. Choosing 'by mistake' misses that these sugars are the third largest solid part of the milk.

worksheets.title: Germ or neighbour? Evidence and open questions

items.p: A bacterium is harmless in the gut and harmful in the bladder. What is different?
items.why: She is the same kind of bacterium in both. In the bladder she is in a place where she can multiply and cause illness.

items.p: What is an opportunist?
opts: A microbe harmless in one place, harmful in another
A microbe who is always harmful
A microbe who never harms anyone
A microbe who lives only in soil
items.why: An opportunist causes illness only when she reaches the wrong place or when the body's defences are low. Many residents are opportunists.

items.p: Growing found 28 kinds of bacteria in tooth film. Reading genes found 59. What does this show?
items.why: Many bacteria will not grow on a laboratory dish, because they need food or air that the dish does not give. Reading genes finds them anyway.

items.p: Carriers of a stomach bacterium have asthma less often. What can we say for certain?
opts: The two are linked, cause unknown
items.why: A link between two things does not show that one causes the other. Carriers may differ from other people in other ways as well. Choosing 'prevents asthma' jumps from a link to a cause.

items.p: Most kinds of microbes on Earth can make a person ill.
items.why: False. A count in 2001 listed 538 kinds of bacteria that make people ill. Human mouths alone hold more than 500 kinds, and soil and sea hold far more.

items.p: Healthy blood has many resident bacteria.
items.why: False. Healthy blood, muscle and brain have no microbes living in them. Defence cells remove any who get through the walls of skin and gut.

items.p: Match each change to what follows from it.
pairs: A thick tooth film gets sweets all day
A splinter pushes skin bacteria in
Feet stay damp in closed shoes
items.why: In each case the microbes were already there. A change of place, numbers, food or neighbours turned them into trouble.

items.p: A count listed 1,415 kinds of germs. Of these, 538 were bacteria. How many were not bacteria?
items.why: 1,415 take away 538 is 877. The rest were fungi, viruses, single-celled beings called protozoa, and worms.

items.p: Bacteria sense how many of their own kind are near. This is called ____ sensing.
items.why: Each bacterium gives out a signal substance. When the signal is strong, all of them change what they do, such as making light.

items.p: Sort these statements: agreed by scientists, or still argued about?
items: Residents make it harder for germs to settle
Most kinds of microbes are not germs
The stomach bacterium protects against asthma
A host and their microbes are one being
items.why: The first three have been measured many times. The last three have evidence on both sides, or depend on what the words mean.

items.p: Give three facts which show that most bacteria are not germs.
items.a: Any three. About 38 trillion bacteria live in a healthy grown-up. Human mouths hold more than 500 kinds. Only 538 kinds of bacteria were on a list of those that make people ill. Gut bacteria break down fibre for us. Skin residents make substances that kill harmful bacteria.
items.why: A strong answer uses numbers or named examples, and does not only say that bacteria are good.

items.p: Fresh sweat has no smell. Hours later a sock smells. Explain what happened in between.
items.a: Bacteria living on the foot fed on substances in the sweat and multiplied in the warm, damp sock. They gave off smelly substances. The smell comes from what the bacteria make.
items.why: A strong answer names the bacteria, the damp place and the time they needed.

items.p: Plan a test: do toe gaps carry more microbes after a day in closed shoes than after a day in sandals?
items.a: Swab the same toe gap in the same way on two evenings, once after shoes and once after sandals. Wipe each bud on a slice from the same boiled potato and seal the bags. Add a slice with no skin. Count the spots after three days. Repeat on other days, because one result can be a fluke.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the footwear, keeps a slice with no skin, and repeats the test.

items.p: A stomach bacterium has lived with humans for 58,000 years. Should doctors remove her from everyone?

views.says: Where she causes ulcers or raises the chance of cancer, yes. An illness we can prevent should be prevented.

views.who: A scientist who studies old residents
views.says: Not from everyone. She has been with us so long that our stomachs may be used to her. We do not yet know what we would lose.
Treat the people who are ill. For healthy carriers, study more before deciding.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The bacterium does cause ulcers and cancer in some carriers. Most carriers never fall ill. Whether she does any good is still argued about.
items.why: A strong answer keeps apart what is known (she causes ulcers) and what is not yet known (whether she also protects).

items.p: Draw the same bacterium twice: once where she is harmless, and once where she is trouble. Label what changed.
items.a: For example: a gut bacterium in the large intestine, harmless, and the same bacterium in the bladder, causing an infection. The label says that the place changed.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same microbe both times and names the change: place, numbers, food or neighbours.
items.art: Two blank circles side by side with a blank label line between them.

quiz.p: Which of these is a resident of your body?
opts: Bacteria deep in your skin pores
Bacteria in a spoon of soil
quiz.why: Bacteria deep in the pores live and multiply there for years. Soil bacteria on fingers are visitors, and soap removes them.

quiz.p: Why do different parts of your skin hold different microbes?
opts: They are washed at different times
They give different water, oil and air
quiz.why: A dry forearm, an oily forehead and a damp toe gap give different food and water, so different microbes do well in each. Washing changes the numbers for a while, but not who lives where.

quiz.p: Why are bacteria so few in the stomach?
quiz.why: Stomach acid kills most of the bacteria swallowed with saliva. The stomach is warm and has food, so acid is what keeps the numbers low.

quiz.p: A swab from an oily forehead grows few spots on potato. What is the best explanation?
opts: Oil-eaters do not grow on potato in air
quiz.why: The commonest forehead bacteria eat skin oil and avoid oxygen, so a potato slice in air does not suit them. Choosing 'no microbes live there' trusts the slice too much.

quiz.p: In a fair swab test, what should be the only thing that differs between the slices?
opts: The place on the skin that was swabbed
quiz.why: Everything else is kept the same, so that any difference in spots comes from the place on the skin.

quiz.p: A harmful bacterium lands in a gut that is full of residents. What usually happens?
opts: She finds little room or food
quiz.why: The residents already cover the surface and use the food, and some make substances that stop her. Most newcomers fail to settle.

quiz.p: After a long course of antibiotics, why can one tough bacterium take over the gut?
quiz.why: The antibiotic kills many residents and leaves room and food. A bacterium who survives the medicine can then multiply with nobody in her way.

quiz.p: Most kinds of microbes never make people ill.
quiz.why: True. The list of microbes known to make people ill is short beside the number of kinds living harmlessly on us, in soil and in the sea.

quiz.p: Which of these microbes is harmful wherever she grows in a person?
quiz.why: The cholera bacterium causes illness whenever she multiplies in a person's gut. The other three are harmless or helpful in their usual places.

quiz.p: Where do a newborn baby's first microbes come from?
opts: They are made by the baby's body
From the baby's first solid food
From the mother and people who hold the baby
quiz.why: A baby meets her first microbes at birth, from her mother and from everyone and everything that touches her. A body does not make microbes: every microbe comes from another microbe.

quiz.p: Which change brings many new kinds of microbes into a baby's gut?
quiz.why: Solid food brings fibre and other new foods for microbes, and new kinds settle. Milk alone feeds only a few kinds.

quiz.p: People who live in one home share microbes most on which part of the body?
quiz.why: Skin touches people, pets and furniture directly all day. A study of 60 families found the strongest sharing on the skin.

quiz.p: Which of these is still argued about by scientists?
quiz.why: One study found that a probiotic slowed the return of a person's own gut community after antibiotics. Other studies find some benefits. The other three are settled.

People who raise orphaned elephant calves give them dung from healthy grown-up elephants, so that the calves gain gut microbes.
Dentists advise brushing to keep the film on teeth thin, and they do not try to remove every bacterium from the mouth.
Police scientists are studying whether the microbes a person leaves on objects could show who touched them.

open_questions.q: Do the microbes we pick up from family, pets and furniture settle on us, or do they only pass through?
open_questions.why_open: Studies can show that people in one home carry the same kinds. They cannot yet tell a microbe who has settled from one who landed an hour ago.

open_questions.q: What do most of our residents do for us, if anything?
open_questions.why_open: A few helpers are well studied. For most of the hundreds of kinds on a body, nobody has tested what happens when they are missing.

open_questions.q: Why does the stomach bacterium cause ulcers in some carriers and no illness in most?
open_questions.why_open: The bacterium comes in different types, people differ, and food and other microbes may matter. No one can yet tell in advance who will fall ill.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to help gut residents return after antibiotics?
open_questions.why_open: Time alone brings most of them back. In one study a probiotic slowed the return. Larger and longer studies have not been done.

open_questions.q: Are people in cities losing kinds of gut microbes, and does it matter for health?
open_questions.why_open: People who hunt and gather carry kinds that are rare in cities. But nobody has shown that carrying fewer kinds causes any illness.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a bacterium who senses her neighbours and acts with them?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure the signals and what the bacteria do next. Nobody has a way to find out what, if anything, a bacterium experiences.

maths.problem: In one family's Three Lands Test, the toe gap slice grew 36 spots, the forearm slice 9 and the No skin slice 1. How many times as many spots grew on the toe gap slice as on the forearm slice? Then take 1 spot away from each skin slice, for what grew without skin, and work it out again.
maths.answer: 4 times. After taking 1 away from each, it is 35 and 8, which is a little more than 4 times.
maths.explain: 36 divided by 9 is 4. After taking away the No skin spot, 35 divided by 8 is 4 with 3 left over, which is about 4.4. The answer hardly changes, because the No skin slice grew so few.
maths.context: This is about the Three Lands Test. In it, you swab three places on your skin and count the spots that grow on potato slices.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'four times as many' compares two places much more clearly than two separate numbers. Taking away the No skin count shows how much of the result really came from skin.

maths.problem: In Hold the Space, three full-gut games ended with 0, 1 and 0 newcomers. Three after-antibiotic games ended with 14, 17 and 11. Find the average for each kind of game. Why is an average of three games better than one game?
maths.answer: The full-gut average is one third of a newcomer, or about 0.3. The after-antibiotic average is 14.
maths.explain: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 divided by 3 is one third. 14 + 17 + 11 = 42, and 42 divided by 3 is 14. Dice are chancy, so one game can come out unusually high or low. An average evens that out.
maths.context: This is about Hold the Space, the dice game in which rice grains are residents and beans are harmful newcomers on a grid of 36 squares.
maths.why_maths: One game depends on luck. An average over several games shows the pattern that the rules produce.

maths.problem: In an after-antibiotic game of Hold the Space, one newcomer lands in round 1. Each newcomer adds one more every round, if there is room. How many newcomers would there be after rounds 2, 3, 4 and 5? In real games the count is usually lower. Why?
maths.answer: 2, 4, 8 and 16. Real games fall behind because some newcomers have no empty square beside them.
maths.explain: The number doubles each round: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. On the grid, a newcomer in a corner or hemmed in by others has no empty square that touches hers, so she cannot add one.
maths.context: This is about Hold the Space, the dice game in which beans stand for harmful newcomers who multiply on a grid.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows how fast microbes can spread when nothing is in the way. Comparing it with the real game shows what crowding does.

maths.problem: A grown-up's skin holds about 100 billion bacteria. The whole body holds about 38 trillion. One trillion is 1,000 billion. About how many times as many bacteria are in the whole body as on the skin?
maths.explain: 38 trillion is 38,000 billion. 38,000 billion divided by 100 billion is 380. So the skin holds less than one part in three hundred of the body's bacteria.
maths.context: This is about where a body's bacteria live. Nearly all of them are in the large intestine, and far fewer are on the skin.
maths.why_maths: Billions and trillions both sound huge. Dividing one by the other shows that the skin, the part we see, holds a tiny share.

maths.problem: A millilitre of stomach contents holds about 10,000 bacteria. A millilitre of saliva holds about 1,000,000,000. A millilitre of large intestine contents holds about 100,000,000,000. How many times as many are in the large intestine as in saliva? How many zeros does each number have?
maths.answer: 100 times as many. The numbers have 4, 9 and 11 zeros.
maths.explain: The large intestine number has two more zeros than the saliva number, and each extra zero means ten times as many. Ten times ten is 100.
maths.context: This is about how the number of bacteria changes along the food tube, from the acid stomach to the crowded large intestine.
maths.why_maths: Counting zeros lets you compare very large numbers quickly, without writing them all out.

maths.problem: In Count the Kinds, 538 of the 1,415 kinds of germs were bacteria. Is that more or less than one third? Viruses and prions made up 217 kinds. Is that more or less than one sixth?
maths.answer: 538 is a little more than one third. 217 is a little less than one sixth.
maths.explain: One third of 1,415 is about 472, and 538 is more than that. One sixth of 1,415 is about 236, and 217 is less than that.
maths.context: This is about Count the Kinds, in which you colour squares to compare the kinds of microbes that make people ill with the kinds that live harmlessly on us.
maths.why_maths: Fractions show how a list is shared out. Here they show that bacteria are only about a third of the germs, although people often use 'germ' and 'bacteria' as the same word.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out who really lives on a human body? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For about a hundred years, scientists listed the microbes of the human body in one way. They wiped a swab on a dish of food jelly and studied whatever grew. By the 1980s there was a puzzle. Under a microscope a sample showed far more cells than ever grew on dishes. In 1985 James Staley and Allan Konopka named this the great plate count anomaly. Meanwhile, in the 1970s, Carl Woese had shown that every living cell carries one gene that works like a name tag. Scientists began to read that gene straight from a sample, without growing anything. In 1999 Ian Kroes, Paul Lepp and David Relman tried both methods on the film from below one man's gums. Growing found 28 kinds of bacteria. Reading genes found 59, and only about a quarter of those had also grown. In 2005 Paul Eckburg, Elisabeth Bik and their team did the same for the gut. Most of the bacteria they found belonged to kinds that had never been grown. In 2012 the Human Microbiome Project published gene readings from many places on the bodies of healthy volunteers.
how_we_found_out.who: James Staley and Allan Konopka. Carl Woese. Ian Kroes, Paul Lepp and David Relman at Stanford University. Paul Eckburg, Elisabeth Bik and their team. The Human Microbiome Project.
how_we_found_out.when: The puzzle was named in 1985. The tooth film study was in 1999, the gut study in 2005, and the Human Microbiome Project's main report in 2012.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the microbes who grow on a laboratory dish are the full list of who lives on us. Reading genes showed that dishes miss most kinds, because many microbes need food or air that a dish does not give.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist holding a glass dish with a few spots in one hand and a long printed strip of DNA letters in the other, looking from one to the other.

roots.context: We have swabbed our own skin and learned who lives on and in a body. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves, about life and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Three Lands Test, swabs from your forearm, your forehead and between your toes grew different numbers and kinds of spots. All three places are your own skin. Scientists who read microbe genes find that the place on the body decides the community more than the person does. A newborn carries nearly the same microbes all over, and the places then sort them. So to a microbe your body is many lands, each with different weather.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'my body' as if a body were one thing and one place. For the beings who live on a body, a dry forearm and a damp underarm are as unlike as a desert and a rainforest. What we count as one is a whole country to them.
deep_truth.evidence: Grice and Segre's team swabbed 20 skin places on 10 people in 2009 and found that dry, damp and oily places each had their own community. Costello's team found in the same year that the body place decided the community more than the person did. Dominguez-Bello's team found in 2010 that newborns carry nearly the same community all over. If your own slices came out differently from what you expected, write down what you got and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are someone, and you are also somewhere. Others are born, eat and die in the lands of your skin and gut, and most of them never leave.
three.what_is_life: No animal has ever lived alone. Animals appeared in seas that bacteria had already filled for more than two billion years, and every animal body since has carried them.
three.what_is_this_world: Water, food and air decide who lives in a forest and who lives in a desert. The same three things decide who lives in your toe gap and who lives on your forearm.

roots.thread: All life on Earth descends from the same first cells. Some of their descendants stayed as single cells. Others, much later, became bodies made of trillions of cells. Then the two came together again, because the single cells settled on the bodies. So when bacteria settle on a newborn, two branches of one very old family are meeting. The body gives land, and the bacteria become part of how the body lives.

teachings.source: Bhagavad Gita 13.1 (numbered 13.2 in editions that count Arjuna's question as the first verse)
teachings.teaching: This body is called the field. The one who knows the field is called the knower of the field.
teachings.link: The Gita means the field in which a person's actions and experiences take place, and it does not speak of microbes. The science in this lesson found that a body is also a field in a plain sense. It is ground on which many beings grow, each in the patch that suits them.

teachings.teaching: To share your food and to care for the many living beings is the chief of all the teachings.
teachings.link: A body already does this. The fibre in your meal that you cannot digest feeds the bacteria of your large intestine. A mother's milk holds sugars that feed her baby's bacteria and that the baby cannot digest.

teachings.source: John Donne, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624), Meditation 17
teachings.teaching: No man is an island, entire of itself. Every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.
teachings.link: Donne meant that people's lives are joined to each other. The science in this lesson found that bodies are joined too. People in one home share skin microbes with each other and with their dog.

science.text: The place on a body decides which microbes live there more than the person does.
Whether a host and all their microbes should be counted as one unit that evolves together is argued about among biologists.
Nobody knows what share of the microbes on a healthy body help, what share harm, and what share simply live there.

other_view.who: Nancy Moran and Daniel Sloan, biologists who study insects and their microbes
other_view.view: They warn against treating a body and all its microbes as one being. Most microbes on a body are picked up from the surroundings and live there for their own sake. Many did not evolve to help their host, and some compete with each other or do harm. In this view you are one animal, and the microbes are separate beings who happen to live on you. Each should be studied as themselves.

practice.title: A hand on the busiest land
practice.say: Lie on your back and put one hand flat on your belly, below your navel. Breathe in slowly and feel your hand rise. Breathe out and feel your hand sink. A few centimetres under your palm is your large intestine. More living beings are there than there are people on Earth. They have been with you since your first days. Breathe ten slow breaths and keep them company. You need not do anything else.
practice.kid: Lie down. Put one hand on your belly, below your navel. Breathe in and feel your hand rise. Breathe out and feel your hand sink. Your large intestine is under your palm. Trillions of tiny beings live there. Take ten slow breaths with them.

ask: Trillions of others live on you. Is your body a someone or a somewhere? Could one thing be both?
To a microbe, your toe gap and your forearm are different lands. What makes two places different places?
A bacterium helps in the gut and harms in the bladder. Is 'good or bad' the right question to ask about her?
Most of your microbes were given to you by others, and you pass yours on. What else about you was given and passed on?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step for a family in a city flat. None has been tried at home from here, so the results below are expected, not measured. The Three Lands Test (the main investigation) needs one potato, four zip bags and four cotton buds. In a warm room spots should show within two days. The usual result is that the toe gap slice grows the most and the forearm slice far fewer, but a child's result may differ, and the steps say to record what really grows. A child's forehead is not yet oily, so that slice is the least predictable. The No skin slice often grows a spot or two, or a dull film, from potato bacteria that survive boiling. If every slice looks the same, boil a fresh potato for longer and repeat. The bags are never opened and a grown-up throws them away. Hold the Space was checked by running its rules 4,000 times on a computer for each kind of game. Full-gut games ended with no newcomers about seven times in ten, and almost never with more than one. After-antibiotic games mostly ended with 9 to 20 newcomers. Six games take about 25 minutes. The Sniff Test depends on real sweat and a pair of socks worn all day, which are easy to find. Count the Kinds, New Land, Who Shares My Microbes? and the 99.9 Percent Label need only paper and things already at home. Both card games have every card written out. No part needs a garden. Facts checked on 19 Nov 2026 against the papers themselves or their published summaries: the skin study of 20 places on 10 people and its rainforest and desert comparison, the finding that body place matters more than the person, the counts of bacteria by organ, the children and adults skin study, the 28 and 59 kinds in tooth film, the newborn study, the milk sugars, the 903 children of the TEDDY study, the nose bacterium and its substance, the 13 of 16 and 4 of 13 patients, the 1,415 kinds of germs, the five-day antibiotic study, the 60 families and their dogs, the 80 million bacteria in a kiss, the personal cloud, the squid's first 10 to 12 hours, the 1970 light-making study, the 58,000 years, the 7,663 adults, the 19 handwash chemicals, the 553 mouth kinds and the elephant handbook. Kural 322, Bhagavad Gita 13.1 and Donne's Meditation 17 were checked against published texts, and the English lines are plain paraphrases or modern spellings. Not checked from here, and written from general knowledge: Carl Woese's work in the 1970s, the story that Lynn Margulis's paper was turned down by about fifteen journals, the ages of the oldest life and the first animals, that cows and termites depend on gut microbes, that bacteria first made the oxygen in the air, the present view that a healthy womb has no microbes, Bonnie Bassler's findings on signals between kinds of bacteria, and the lengths of the three videos. The story's elephant camp and its people are made up.
